Anabaptist (Mennonite, Amish, Brethren).beliefs: God created the world; salvation comes by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, shown in a life of discipleship (Nachfolge). Believers look to eternal life with God and the resurrection. Authority rests on the Bible, especially the Sermon on the Mount, read together by the gathered church; Old Order groups also follow the community's Ordnung (unwritten rules).
Anabaptist (Mennonite, Amish, Brethren).values: Following Jesus in daily life; adult (believer's) baptism; nonresistance and peacemaking; humility (Gelassenheit, yielding to God); simplicity; mutual aid; service; community discipline.
Anabaptist (Mennonite, Amish, Brethren).forbids: Violence, military service and revenge; swearing oaths; pride and worldliness; for Old Order groups, much modern technology and outside media; sexual immorality; occult practice.
Anabaptist (Mennonite, Amish, Brethren).family: Marriage is one man and one woman for life; large, close families in conservative groups; plain dress and head coverings for women in Amish and conservative Mennonite communities; distinct gender roles in conservative groups. Identity is marked by adult baptism, plain dress, Pennsylvania German among the Amish, separation from the world and service work (Mennonite Central Committee).
Anabaptist (Mennonite, Amish, Brethren).stories: Conservative communities read mainly Scripture, the Martyrs Mirror and wholesome stories and avoid TV and film; more modern Mennonites engage with literature and art. Violence shown as heroic conflicts with nonresistance.
Anabaptist (Mennonite, Amish, Brethren).range: Old Order Amish and conservative Mennonites (strict separation) to Mennonite Church USA (progressive).
Anabaptist (Mennonite, Amish, Brethren).sources: Schleitheim Confession (1527); Dordrecht Confession (1632); Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995).

topics.Alcohol: Many abstain; drunkenness forbidden.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Drugs forbidden; tobacco discouraged (some Old Order exceptions).
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Occult forbidden; conservative groups avoid much fantasy media.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Christ only; nonresistant witness.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Pacifism and nonresistance (Matthew 5:39): violence, war and revenge shown as heroic are often a significant concern.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Modesty and plain dress; sexual content a significant concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Traditional in conservative groups; MC USA moving toward affirming.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Submission to church community; separation from "the world."
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Hope in resurrection; suicide treated with grief and care.
topics.Lying and deception: Truthfulness and refusal of oaths; lying a serious concern.

Anabaptist (Mennonite, Amish, Brethren).media: Separation from the world (Schleitheim Confession, Article 4) leads Old Order groups to avoid TV and most popular media. Mennonite Church USA is much more open. Violence shown as heroic is the central concern across the range.

Anglican / Episcopal.beliefs: God the Holy Trinity created the world; salvation is through Jesus Christ; Christians hope for resurrection and eternal life. Authority rests on Scripture, interpreted with tradition and reason (the "three-legged stool"), and is expressed in the creeds and the Book of Common Prayer ("the law of prayer is the law of belief").
Anglican / Episcopal.values: Common worship and the sacraments of baptism and Eucharist; prayer; the via media (middle way); service and justice; hospitality.
Anglican / Episcopal.forbids: The Ten Commandments and the baptismal promises: renouncing evil, respecting the dignity of every human being; occult practice and sexual sin as defined in each province.
Anglican / Episcopal.family: Marriage is a lifelong covenant; the Episcopal Church allows same-sex marriage (2015), while ACNA and most of the Global South provinces hold to marriage between a man and a woman. Identity is marked by baptism, confirmation, the liturgical year and the Prayer Book.
Anglican / Episcopal.stories: A strong tradition of literature, music and art (including C.S. Lewis as an Anglican writer); fiction is judged by its moral vision.
Anglican / Episcopal.range: Episcopal Church (progressive) to ACNA and global Anglicans (conservative).
Anglican / Episcopal.sources: Book of Common Prayer; Thirty-Nine Articles; Lambeth resolutions; ACNA catechism "To Be a Christian."

topics.Alcohol: Moderate use normal; drunkenness sinful.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Occult forbidden; fantasy literature has deep Anglican roots (C.S. Lewis).
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Respect for other faiths; Christ as Lord.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Just war (Article 37); revenge rejected.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Chastity; content judged case by case.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Episcopal Church affirming; ACNA traditional.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Honor parents and lawful authority (Catechism).
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Resurrection; suicide treated pastorally.

Anglican / Episcopal.media: A strong literary tradition (C.S. Lewis, Dorothy Sayers) sees imagination as a gift. Works are judged by how they frame good and evil rather than by what they show. Practice ranges from progressive to conservative.

Bahá'í.beliefs: One unknowable God has sent a series of Manifestations (including Abraham, Moses, Krishna, Buddha, Jesus, Muhammad, the Báb and Bahá'u'lláh) in progressive revelation. The purpose of life is to know and worship God and to develop spiritual qualities; the soul continues after death and progresses toward God; heaven and hell are states of nearness or distance. Authority rests on the writings of Bahá'u'lláh, the Báb and 'Abdu'l-Bahá, the interpretations of Shoghi Effendi, and the elected Universal House of Justice.
Bahá'í.values: The oneness of God, religion and humanity; daily obligatory prayer and reading of scripture; the 19-day fast; truthfulness, chastity, service, consultation; equality of women and men; harmony of science and religion; universal education.
Bahá'í.forbids: Alcohol and drugs; gambling; backbiting; sex outside marriage; partisan politics; prejudice of any kind; magic and occult practice.
Bahá'í.family: Marriage between a man and a woman, requiring parental consent; chastity before marriage; modesty and moderation. Identity is marked by Nineteen-Day Feasts, holy days, the fast in March, and service activities such as children's classes and study circles.
Bahá'í.stories: The arts are praised as worship when practiced in a spirit of service; entertainment is a matter of conscience guided by chastity, dignity and avoiding prejudice.
Bahá'í.range: One worldwide community guided by the Universal House of Justice; individual conscience on most entertainment.
Bahá'í.sources: Kitab-i-Aqdas; writings of Baha'u'llah, 'Abdu'l-Baha and Shoghi Effendi ("The Advent of Divine Justice" on a chaste and holy life); Universal House of Justice letters.

topics.Alcohol: Forbidden.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Drugs forbidden except as medicine; tobacco discouraged.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Spiritualism and occult discouraged; fantasy acceptable (to verify).
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Progressive revelation: all major faiths from one God; mockery of any faith a concern.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Strong commitment to non-violence and unity; holy war abolished.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Chastity before marriage; modesty.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Sexual relations only within marriage of a man and a woman; prejudice against anyone rejected.
topics.Gender roles and family: Equality of women and men is a core principle.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Obedience to government; non-partisan.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: The soul progresses after death; suicide forbidden.
topics.Lying and deception: Truthfulness is "the foundation of all human virtues."

Bahá'í.media: Arts are praised as worship when done in service. Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" warns against degrading art, literature and entertainment (to verify exact wording).

Baptist.beliefs: God created all things; humanity fell into sin and is saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ alone. Believers will live with God forever in heaven; those who reject Christ face eternal separation in hell. The Bible is the sole and sufficient authority; each local congregation is self-governing, and every believer may read and interpret Scripture (soul competency).
Baptist.values: Personal conversion and believer's baptism by immersion; evangelism and missions; Bible reading and prayer; church membership; religious liberty; holy living.
Baptist.forbids: Sexual immorality and pornography, drunkenness (many Baptists abstain from alcohol), occult practice, blasphemy and profanity, and media that glorify sin.
Baptist.family: Marriage is one man and one woman for life; sex belongs within marriage; the Baptist Faith and Message 2000 teaches complementary roles of husband and wife and limits the office of pastor to men. Identity is marked by a testimony of faith, believer's baptism, Sunday worship, Sunday school and church community.
Baptist.stories: Stories and media are judged by whether they honor God and do not lead into sin; fantasy is accepted by many, while some avoid magic and occult themes.
Baptist.range: Wide range: Southern Baptist, Independent Fundamental, American Baptist (more progressive), Reformed Baptist. Each congregation is self-governing.
Baptist.sources: Baptist Faith and Message 2000 (SBC); 1689 London Baptist Confession (Reformed Baptists); SBC resolutions on alcohol, entertainment and media; Focus on the Family / Plugged In (evangelical media guide used widely by Baptists).

topics.Alcohol: Many Baptists are teetotal (SBC resolutions urge abstinence, e.g. 2006); others drink in moderation. Alcohol shown positively is often a concern.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Drugs and drunkenness condemned; tobacco discouraged.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Witchcraft and occult forbidden (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); fantasy magic is debated, and many families are cautious, especially with spells, summoning and spirits.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Exclusive claims of Christ (John 14:6); other religions' gods shown as real or good can be a concern.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Just war generally accepted; revenge rejected (Romans 12:19); graphic violence a concern.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Strong emphasis on purity and modesty; sexual content and fan service often a major concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Marriage is one man and one woman (BF&M 2000, Article XVIII); same-sex romance and gender transition usually a significant concern.
topics.Gender roles and family: Complementarian roles in home and church (BF&M 2000).
topics.Language and blasphemy: Profanity and taking God's name in vain a common concern (Ephesians 4:29; Exodus 20:7).
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Obedience to parents (Ephesians 6:1); respect for authority.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Salvation by faith; heaven and hell real; suicide treated with grief and pastoral care.
topics.Lying and deception: Lying sinful (Proverbs 12:22); deceptive heroes worth discussing.

Baptist.media: Philippians 4:8 ("whatever is true... pure... lovely") is the common test. SBC resolutions have criticized entertainment content (for example the 1997 Disney boycott). Soul liberty means each family decides, and Plugged In is widely used.

Buddhist.beliefs: The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths: life involves suffering (dukkha), suffering arises from craving, it can end (nirvana), and the Noble Eightfold Path leads there. There is no creator God in most schools; beings are reborn according to karma until liberation. Authority rests on the Buddha's teachings (Dharma), the scriptures of each school and the community of monks and teachers (Sangha): the Three Jewels.
Buddhist.values: Compassion (karuna), loving-kindness (metta), wisdom, mindfulness and meditation, generosity, non-attachment and right livelihood.
Buddhist.forbids: The Five Precepts: no killing or harming living beings, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, no intoxicants that cloud the mind. Media that stir hatred, craving or cruelty are discouraged.
Buddhist.family: Marriage is a civil and family matter rather than a sacrament; sexual misconduct (harmful or exploitative sex) is to be avoided; views on same-sex relationships vary by teacher and culture. Identity is marked by taking refuge in the Three Jewels, temple visits, festivals such as Vesak, offerings and meditation.
Buddhist.stories: The Jataka tales and other teaching stories use fiction freely; images of the Buddha and deities are devotional aids. Violence is judged by the intention and karma it shows; gods and spirits are common in Buddhist cosmology.
Buddhist.range: Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana and Japanese schools; lay practice varies.
Buddhist.sources: The Five Precepts; Dhammapada; teachings of the various schools; Buddhist parenting resources.

topics.Alcohol: Fifth precept: refrain from intoxicants.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Spirits common in folk practice; not usually a concern.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Pluralistic; Buddhist imagery used carelessly may concern some.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: First precept: non-harm; violence and revenge seen as creating suffering.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Third precept: avoid sexual misconduct.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Views vary; many traditions accepting.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Right speech: harsh and false speech discouraged.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Respect for teachers and elders.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Rebirth and karma; suicide discouraged.
topics.Lying and deception: Fourth precept: refrain from false speech.

Buddhist.media: Right speech and mindfulness of what feeds the mind guide choices. On observance days lay people often take the eight precepts, which include abstaining from shows and entertainment. Monastics avoid entertainment.

Catholic.beliefs: God created the world good, out of love; humans, made in God's image, are called to share eternal life with God through Jesus Christ. Death is followed by judgment: heaven, purgatory as purification, or hell as self-chosen separation from God; the dead will rise at the end of time. Authority rests on Scripture and Sacred Tradition, interpreted by the Magisterium (the Pope and bishops in communion with him).
Catholic.values: Faith, hope and charity; the seven sacraments, above all the Eucharist (Sunday Mass); prayer; the works of mercy; the dignity of every human life; the common good and care for the poor.
Catholic.forbids: The Ten Commandments as taught in the Catechism: idolatry, occult practices and divination, blasphemy, murder, sexual sin and pornography, theft, lying and calumny. Media that glamorize sin or degrade persons are discouraged.
Catholic.family: Marriage is a lifelong sacramental union of one man and one woman, open to children; sex belongs within marriage; chastity and modesty are virtues for all. The Church teaches that sex is given by God and not chosen. Identity is marked by baptism, first Communion, confirmation, saints' days, the liturgical year and Friday abstinence in Lent.
Catholic.stories: The Church has long commissioned art and values beauty as a path to God. Fiction may depict evil when it serves truth and does not invite the viewer to share in it; occult practice, not its depiction in a story, is what is forbidden.
Catholic.range: Practice ranges from traditionalist to progressive parishes; the Catechism is the shared reference.
Catholic.sources: Catechism of the Catholic Church (CCC); papal documents; USCCB movie and media reviews; Pontifical Council for Social Communications, "Ethics in Communications" (2000).

topics.Alcohol: Permitted in moderation; drunkenness is sinful (CCC 2290).
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Drug abuse is a grave offense (CCC 2291); tobacco in moderation not forbidden.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Divination, magic and spiritism are forbidden (CCC 2115-2117); fantasy magic as story element is often tolerated, and judged by how it is framed.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Respect for what is true in other religions (Nostra Aetate); concern if presented as equally true or if mocking the faith.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Just-war teaching; self-defense allowed (CCC 2263-2265, 2309); revenge rejected; gratuitous violence in media criticized.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Chastity and modesty (CCC 2337-2359, 2521-2524); pornography grave matter (CCC 2354); fan service a common concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Same-sex acts not approved (CCC 2357-2359) while calling for respect for persons; gender ideology questioned (Dicastery documents, 2024).
topics.Gender roles and family: Complementarity of men and women; marriage between a man and a woman; strong pro-family emphasis.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Taking the Lord's name in vain forbidden (CCC 2142-2155); coarse language a lesser concern.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Honor parents (CCC 2214-2220); legitimate authority respected; unjust authority may be resisted.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Hope of resurrection; suicide gravely contrary to love of self but judgment left to God (CCC 2280-2283); purgatory, saints.
topics.Lying and deception: Lying is wrong (CCC 2482-2486); stories may depict it, framing matters.

Catholic.media: Vatican II's Inter Mirifica (1963), Communio et Progressio (1971) and "Ethics in Communications" (2000) hold that media should serve truth, dignity and the common good. Depicting evil is acceptable when it serves understanding and is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7). John Paul II's Letter to Artists (1999) praises art that seeks beauty. CCC 2493-2499 and 2525 address media and permissiveness.

Christian Science.beliefs: God is infinite Mind, Spirit, Life, Truth, Love; God's creation is wholly spiritual and good, and humans are God's spiritual image and likeness. Sin, sickness and death are not part of God's creation and are overcome through understanding God, as Jesus showed. Life continues after what appears as death, as a progressing spiritual existence. Authority rests on the Bible and Mary Baker Eddy's Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, the church's "pastor".
Christian Science.values: Prayer-based spiritual healing; daily study of the weekly Bible Lesson; gratitude, purity, love and spiritual understanding; Christian Science practitioners and the Sunday School.
Christian Science.forbids: Alcohol and tobacco; reliance on "material" thinking; Mrs. Eddy warned against hypnotism, mesmerism and spiritualism. Members generally rely on prayer rather than medical treatment, as their choice.
Christian Science.family: Marriage is honored; purity and moral conduct are expected. Identity is marked by church membership, Sunday School until age 20, Wednesday testimony meetings, the Christian Science Monitor and Reading Rooms.
Christian Science.stories: No formal content code; members are encouraged to watch over thought and to avoid fear-inducing or degrading images, while embracing what is good and uplifting.
Christian Science.range: Church of Christ, Scientist (The Mother Church, Boston) and branch churches; members vary in practice.
Christian Science.sources: Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures (Mary Baker Eddy); Manual of The Mother Church; Christian Science Journal and Sentinel.

topics.Alcohol: Members abstain from alcohol (Church Manual).
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Members abstain from tobacco and drugs; reliance on prayer for healing is central, and members decide about medical care.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Mesmerism, spiritualism and "animal magnetism" rejected as error.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Respect for other faiths; God understood as divine Mind, Spirit, Love.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: No formal pacifism; violence seen as a false belief to be overcome.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Purity and marriage valued.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Less public teaching than many churches; families vary (to verify).
topics.Gender roles and family: Founded by a woman; women and men serve equally as Readers and practitioners.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Respect for parents; spiritual self-government emphasized.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Life is spiritual and death is ultimately unreal; strong focus on healing.

Christian Science.media: Thought shapes experience, so members guard what they dwell on ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392). Depictions of fear, disease and sin are seen as mental influences to be guarded against.

Conservative Jewish.beliefs: One God created the world and entered into covenant with the Jewish people; Torah is understood as divinely inspired and transmitted through a human, historical process. Halakha is binding and develops over time through rabbinic interpretation. Beliefs about the afterlife (olam haba, resurrection) are affirmed in the liturgy and interpreted variously. Authority rests with Torah, Talmud and codes, interpreted by the Rabbinical Assembly's Committee on Jewish Law and Standards (CJLS) and the local rabbi (mara d'atra).
Conservative Jewish.values: Torah study, Shabbat, kashrut, prayer, tikkun olam (repairing the world), tzedakah, Hebrew and Jewish peoplehood, Israel, lifelong learning.
Conservative Jewish.forbids: Idolatry and sorcery; Shabbat desecration; non-kosher food; harmful and vulgar speech (lashon hara, nivul peh); degrading sexual content.
Conservative Jewish.family: Marriage is kiddushin, a sacred covenant; since 2006 the CJLS permits same-sex marriage and LGBTQ rabbis, and men and women are egalitarian in ritual in most congregations. Identity is marked by brit milah, bar/bat mitzvah, Shabbat and holidays, kashrut and day schools or Hebrew school, Camp Ramah and USY.
Conservative Jewish.stories: Fiction and the arts are broadly welcomed and judged by Jewish ethical values on speech, modesty and dignity.
Conservative Jewish.range: Conservative (Masorti) movement: halakha seen as binding and evolving; the Rabbinical Assembly's Committee on Jewish Law and Standards (CJLS) issues rulings.
Conservative Jewish.sources: Torah and Talmud; CJLS responsa; "Emet Ve-Emunah: Statement of Principles of Conservative Judaism" (1988).

topics.Alcohol: Wine in ritual; moderation.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Drug abuse prohibited; CJLS has ruled smoking prohibited.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Sorcery forbidden; fantasy generally accepted.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Idolatry forbidden; respect for other faiths; antisemitic tropes a key concern.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Self-defense permitted; revenge rejected.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Modesty and sexual ethics within committed relationships.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: CJLS (2006) permitted gay and lesbian rabbis and same-sex commitment ceremonies; views vary by congregation.
topics.Gender roles and family: Egalitarian in most congregations (women ordained since 1985).
topics.Language and blasphemy: Lashon hara and vulgar speech discouraged.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Honor parents; tradition taken seriously.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Beliefs about afterlife vary; suicide met with compassion.

Conservative Jewish.media: No formal media rules. Values such as modesty, kind speech and Jewish dignity are applied by families; antisemitic portrayals are a concern.

Conservative / traditional.beliefs: This is a values frame rather than a religion: families of any faith or none who see inherited institutions (family, faith, nation, community) as carrying tested wisdom. Views on creation and afterlife come from the family's own faith. Authority rests on tradition, the family, religious communities, constitutional order and lived experience, with change made carefully.
Conservative / traditional.values: Duty, honor, loyalty, self-reliance, hard work, patriotism, respect for parents and elders, courage, faith communities and personal responsibility.
Conservative / traditional.forbids: Disrespect for parents and legitimate authority; glamorized crime, drug use and promiscuity; vulgarity; mockery of faith and country; content seen as pushing political messages onto children.
Conservative / traditional.family: The married two-parent family is the foundation of society; sexual restraint and modesty; many see sex differences as natural; parents as the primary authority over children's upbringing. Identity is marked by family, faith, national holidays, military and community service.
Conservative / traditional.stories: Classic stories of heroism, sacrifice and good defeating evil are prized; violence in a just cause is acceptable; concern is with moral relativism, nihilism and gratuitous content.
Conservative / traditional.range: Families of any or no faith who value tradition, duty, patriotism and family structure.
Conservative / traditional.sources: Plugged In; Common Sense Media; Heritage and family-policy publications; classical education resources.

topics.Alcohol: Concern if glamorized for minors.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Varies; some concern about occult themes.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Respect for traditional faith; concern about mockery of religion.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Self-defense and heroism valued; concern about gratuitous gore.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Concern about sexual content and fan service.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Concern when presented to children.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Respect for parents and lawful authority valued; anti-authority messages a concern.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Concern about portrayals of suicide.

Conservative / traditional.media: The classical ideal of "the good, the true and the beautiful" guides choices, with concern about media that undermines family, faith, duty or national tradition.

Eastern Orthodox.beliefs: God the Holy Trinity created the world good; humanity, fallen, is restored in Jesus Christ, and the goal of life is theosis: union with God by grace. The dead await the general resurrection and final judgment. Authority rests on Holy Tradition, which includes Scripture, the seven Ecumenical Councils, the Church Fathers, the liturgy and the icons, as held by the bishops in apostolic succession.
Eastern Orthodox.values: The Divine Liturgy and the Holy Mysteries (sacraments); prayer (including the Jesus Prayer); fasting; repentance and confession; humility; veneration of icons and saints; almsgiving.
Eastern Orthodox.forbids: Occult practices and divination; passions such as lust, anger and pride; sexual immorality; blasphemy; entertainment that inflames the passions or mocks the holy.
Eastern Orthodox.family: Marriage is a sacrament between a man and a woman, an icon of Christ and the Church; chastity and modesty; priesthood for men. Identity is marked by baptism with chrismation and communion in infancy, name days, fasting seasons, Pascha (Easter) and icons in the home.
Eastern Orthodox.stories: Iconography is theology in image; sacred art follows canons. Secular fiction is judged by whether it guards the heart and nurtures virtue or feeds the passions.
Eastern Orthodox.range: Jurisdictions (Greek, Russian, Antiochian, OCA and others) share doctrine; pastoral practice varies by priest and parish.
Eastern Orthodox.sources: Holy Scripture and the Church Fathers; Orthodox Study Bible; "The Orthodox Church" (Ware); jurisdiction catechisms; "Bases of the Social Concept" (Russian Orthodox Church, 2000).

topics.Alcohol: Permitted, often part of feasts; drunkenness condemned.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Drug abuse condemned; smoking discouraged, forbidden for clergy in many places.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Sorcery and occult practice strongly condemned; evil spirits taken as real, so demonic imagery can be a serious concern.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Holds Orthodoxy as the fullness of faith; syncretism and mockery of holy things are concerns.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Killing even in war calls for repentance in the tradition (St. Basil, canon 13); just-war language less used; revenge rejected.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Chastity and modesty; strong concern about sexual imagery and "passions."
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Traditional teaching on marriage and sexuality; gender seen as given.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Blasphemy serious; reverence for holy names and icons.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Obedience to parents and spiritual fathers stressed.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Resurrection; prayer for the dead; suicide traditionally denied church funeral, with pastoral exceptions for illness.
topics.Lying and deception: Lying condemned; deception for others' good debated in the Fathers.

Eastern Orthodox.media: Guarding the senses (nepsis, watchfulness) is a core practice: what one looks at shapes the soul. Holy images are venerated, so mocking icons or sacred things is serious. Fathers such as John Chrysostom warned against the theatre. "Bases of the Social Concept" (2000) asks media to respect moral values.

Hindu.beliefs: The eternal reality (Brahman) underlies all; the universe passes through cycles of creation and dissolution. The soul (atman) is reborn according to karma until liberation (moksha). Life pursues four aims: dharma (duty), artha (prosperity), kama (pleasure) and moksha. Authority rests on the Vedas and Upanishads (shruti), the epics, Puranas and law texts (smriti), and living teachers (gurus) and sampradayas (lineages).
Hindu.values: Dharma suited to one's stage and role; devotion (bhakti) to God in many forms; ahimsa (non-harm); truthfulness; respect for parents, elders and teachers; puja, festivals and pilgrimage; yoga and meditation.
Hindu.forbids: Harm to living beings (many are vegetarian; beef is widely avoided); intoxicants for many; disrespect to deities, scriptures and elders; adharma such as deceit and cruelty.
Hindu.family: Marriage is a sacred samskara; family and lineage are central; modesty is valued, with wide regional variation. Identity is marked by samskaras (naming, sacred thread, marriage), festivals such as Diwali and Holi, home shrines, temple and dietary practice.
Hindu.stories: The Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas are rich in battles, gods, demons and magic, so these are familiar in stories. Concern is mainly disrespectful portrayal of deities and sacred symbols.
Hindu.range: Highly diverse: Vaishnava, Shaiva, Shakta, Smarta traditions; many regional practices.
Hindu.sources: Bhagavad Gita; Dharmashastra; ISKCON and other sampradaya teachings; Hindu American Foundation resources.

topics.Alcohol: Many abstain, especially in devotional traditions; varies.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Spirits and deities part of the worldview; black magic disapproved.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Pluralistic; concern about mockery of deities or Hindu symbols.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Dharma may require righteous fighting (Gita); ahimsa (non-harm) valued.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Modesty valued; varies by community.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Varies; traditional views common, some accepting.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Respect for parents and elders very strong.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Karma and rebirth; suicide discouraged.

Hindu.media: Classical aesthetics (rasa theory, Natya Shastra) values art that evokes emotion. Deities are freely depicted, but mockery or misuse of them is objected to. Some apply the Gita's sattvic, rajasic and tamasic qualities (chapter 17) to media.

Jehovah's Witness.beliefs: Jehovah is the one true God and Creator; Jesus is his Son, the first of his creation, not part of a Trinity. God's Kingdom will soon replace human governments and make the earth a paradise; a "little flock" of 144,000 will rule in heaven, and most faithful people will live forever on earth. There is no immortal soul or hellfire; the dead are unconscious and await resurrection. Authority rests on the Bible (New World Translation), as explained by the Governing Body.
Jehovah's Witness.values: Bible study; Kingdom Hall meetings; preaching from house to house; Christian neutrality in politics and war; moral cleanness; honesty; love among the brotherhood.
Jehovah's Witness.forbids: Blood transfusions; celebrating birthdays and holidays with pagan origins (Christmas, Easter, Halloween); spiritism, magic and occult themes; violence, immorality and bad associations; idolatry, including flag salutes.
Jehovah's Witness.family: Marriage between a man and a woman; the husband as head of the household; sex only within marriage; modest dress. Identity is marked by baptism, field service, meetings and not taking part in holidays and politics.
Jehovah's Witness.stories: Members use Bible-trained conscience in entertainment; the organization warns against content featuring spiritism, demons, magic, violence and immorality, and produces its own videos for children.
Jehovah's Witness.range: One worldwide organization guided by the Governing Body; many entertainment choices are left to personal Bible-trained conscience.
Jehovah's Witness.sources: jw.org articles on entertainment, spiritism and violence; "Keep Yourselves in God's Love"; The Watchtower and Awake!; New World Translation.

topics.Alcohol: Moderate use allowed; drunkenness is a serious sin.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Tobacco, betel nut and recreational drugs forbidden.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Spiritism, magic and demon contact firmly rejected, including in entertainment (jw.org counsel); a major concern.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Only one true worship; holidays with non-biblical origins (Christmas, birthdays, Halloween) not celebrated, so holiday stories may be a concern.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Political neutrality and no military service; violent entertainment discouraged (Psalm 11:5).
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: High moral standards; sexual content and pornography a significant concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Homosexual acts considered sinful; same-sex romance usually a significant concern.
topics.Gender roles and family: Husband as head of household; men take the lead in the congregation.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Obscene speech and misuse of God's name avoided.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Respect for parents; no flag salute or nationalism, so patriotic heroism can be a concern.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: The dead are unconscious; no hellfire; hope of resurrection; suicide treated with compassion.

Jehovah's Witness.media: jw.org counsels asking whether entertainment features what God hates, especially violence (Psalm 11:5), immorality and spiritism (Galatians 5:19-21). Many choices are left to conscience, but magic and occult content is widely avoided.

Latter-day Saint.beliefs: God the Eternal Father, His Son Jesus Christ and the Holy Ghost are three distinct beings. Humans lived with God as spirit children before birth; earth life is a test and a chance to gain a body and grow; through Christ's Atonement all will be resurrected, and most will receive a degree of glory, with exaltation in the celestial kingdom for those who keep covenants. Authority rests on scripture (Bible, Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants, Pearl of Great Price) and continuing revelation through living prophets.
Latter-day Saint.values: Faith in Jesus Christ, repentance, baptism and temple covenants; family home evening and scripture study; service and missionary work; tithing; self-reliance.
Latter-day Saint.forbids: The Word of Wisdom (no alcohol, tobacco, coffee, tea or harmful drugs); the law of chastity; pornography; profanity and taking God's name in vain; Sabbath-breaking; media that are vulgar, immoral or violent.
Latter-day Saint.family: Marriage between a man and a woman, sealed for eternity in the temple; gender is an eternal identity (The Family: A Proclamation to the World); modest dress. Identity is marked by baptism at eight, priesthood, temple worship, missions and ward life.
Latter-day Saint.stories: Members seek "anything virtuous, lovely, or of good report" (13th Article of Faith); For the Strength of Youth asks young people to choose uplifting media.
Latter-day Saint.range: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints; members vary in strictness about media.
Latter-day Saint.sources: "For the Strength of Youth" (2022); Word of Wisdom (Doctrine and Covenants 89); General Handbook; Gospel Topics essays.

topics.Alcohol: Not consumed (Word of Wisdom); alcohol shown positively is a concern.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Tobacco, drugs, coffee and tea not used.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Occult and spirit contact avoided; fantasy commonly enjoyed.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Respect for other faiths (Articles of Faith 11).
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Self-defense and just causes accepted (Alma 43); revenge rejected.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Chastity and modesty strongly emphasized; youth guidance warns against media that is "vulgar, immoral, violent."
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Traditional teaching ("The Family: A Proclamation to the World", 1995).
topics.Gender roles and family: Family central; men and women equal partners with distinct roles (Proclamation).
topics.Language and blasphemy: Profanity and taking God's name in vain avoided (For the Strength of Youth).
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Honor parents; follow prophets and leaders.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Plan of salvation; suicide treated with compassion (Handbook).
topics.Lying and deception: Honesty is a core value (Articles of Faith 13).

Latter-day Saint.media: For the Strength of Youth (2022) asks youth to choose entertainment that invites the Spirit, replacing earlier specific counsel (such as avoiding R-rated films) with principles. Article of Faith 13 seeks what is "virtuous, lovely, or of good report."

Lutheran.beliefs: God created all things; humans are sinners justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ, not by works. Believers look to resurrection and eternal life. Authority rests on Scripture alone, with the Lutheran Confessions (Book of Concord) as its faithful exposition; Word and Sacrament (baptism, Lord's Supper) are the means of grace.
Lutheran.values: The gospel of forgiveness; infant baptism and the Lord's Supper; vocation (serving God in daily work and family); the Small Catechism at home; hymnody and church music.
Lutheran.forbids: The Ten Commandments as explained in Luther's catechisms, including idolatry and witchcraft, misusing God's name, despising parents, murder and hatred, adultery and lust, theft, and gossip or false witness.
Lutheran.family: LCMS and WELS hold marriage as one man and one woman and ordain only men; the ELCA ordains women and permits same-sex marriages. Identity is marked by baptism, confirmation after catechism instruction, the liturgy, hymnody and the church year.
Lutheran.stories: Luther kept images and music in worship; Christian freedom allows wide use of fiction, judged by conscience and the commandments.
Lutheran.range: LCMS and WELS (confessional) differ from ELCA (mainline).
Lutheran.sources: Luther's Small and Large Catechism; Book of Concord; LCMS CTCR reports; ELCA social statements.

topics.Alcohol: Moderate use is normal in the tradition; drunkenness sinful.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Occult forbidden (Large Catechism on the second commandment); fantasy often accepted.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Other religions not saving; respect for neighbors.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Two-kingdoms teaching; just war and lawful authority accepted; revenge rejected.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Chastity (sixth commandment explanation); concern over explicit content.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: LCMS/WELS traditional; ELCA affirming.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Fourth commandment covers parents and authorities.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Resurrection; suicide treated with pastoral care.
topics.Lying and deception: Eighth commandment: "put the best construction on everything."

Lutheran.media: Entertainment is generally adiaphora (neither commanded nor forbidden), judged by love and conscience. Luther valued art and music. Confessional (LCMS, WELS) and mainline (ELCA) families differ in strictness.

Mainline progressive Protestant.beliefs: God created the world and loves it; Jesus Christ reveals God and reconciles humanity; Christians live in hope of resurrection and God's coming reign of justice and peace. Many hold a wider hope for salvation. Authority rests on Scripture read in its historical context, alongside tradition, reason and experience, and decided through denominational assemblies.
Mainline progressive Protestant.values: Love of God and neighbor; justice, peace and care for creation; inclusion and hospitality; worship and sacraments; service, education and ecumenical cooperation.
Mainline progressive Protestant.forbids: Discrimination, exploitation and abuse; violence glorified; harmful stereotypes; dishonesty. Few rules about entertainment itself.
Mainline progressive Protestant.family: Women and LGBTQ people ordained in most of these churches; same-sex marriage affirmed (ELCA, Episcopal, PC(USA), UCC, UMC since 2024); emphasis on faithful, consensual, loving relationships. Identity is marked by baptism, confirmation, the church year and social-justice work.
Mainline progressive Protestant.stories: Fiction and the arts are valued as ways to explore faith and human experience; content concerns focus on cruelty, bigotry and exploitation rather than magic or other religions.
Mainline progressive Protestant.range: ELCA, Episcopal Church, PC(USA), UCC, UMC and Disciples of Christ in their progressive expressions.
Mainline progressive Protestant.sources: Denominational social statements (UCC, ELCA, PC(USA)); progressive Christian educators and reviewers.

topics.Alcohol: Moderation; concern about addiction.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Fantasy and myth usually accepted; occult practice rarely a focus.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Interfaith respect and dialogue valued.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Peace and justice emphasis; concern about glorified violence.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Consent and healthy relationships emphasized; exploitative fan service a concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Affirming of LGBTQ people.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Hurtful and demeaning language a concern more than mild profanity.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Justice can require challenging authority.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Grace-centered; suicide approached with mental-health care.
topics.Lying and deception: Honesty valued; nuance in moral dilemmas.

Mainline progressive Protestant.media: No formal media rules. Works are engaged critically, with attention to representation, justice and how the vulnerable are treated.

Methodist / Wesleyan.beliefs: God created the world; salvation is by grace through faith in Christ, offered to all (prevenient grace); believers can grow toward holiness and perfect love (sanctification). Christians hope for resurrection and eternal life. Authority rests on Scripture as primary, with tradition, reason and experience (the "Wesleyan Quadrilateral").
Methodist / Wesleyan.values: Holiness of heart and life; works of piety (prayer, Scripture, sacraments) and works of mercy; social holiness and service; class meetings and accountability; hymn singing.
Methodist / Wesleyan.forbids: John Wesley's General Rules: do no harm, do good, attend upon the ordinances of God. Holiness churches traditionally discourage alcohol, gambling and worldly amusements; occult practice; sexual sin.
Methodist / Wesleyan.family: Women are ordained across most Wesleyan bodies. The United Methodist Church removed its restrictions on LGBTQ clergy and same-sex weddings in 2024; Global Methodist, Free Methodist, Wesleyan and Nazarene churches hold to marriage between a man and a woman. Identity is marked by baptism, confirmation or membership vows, small groups and hymns of Charles Wesley.
Methodist / Wesleyan.stories: Media are judged by whether they help or hinder growth in holiness and love; holiness churches have been more cautious about film and entertainment.
Methodist / Wesleyan.range: United Methodist (now affirming after 2024), Global Methodist, Free Methodist, Wesleyan, Nazarene (holiness).
Methodist / Wesleyan.sources: Wesley's General Rules; UMC Book of Discipline and Social Principles; Global Methodist Book of Doctrines and Discipline; Church of the Nazarene Manual.

topics.Alcohol: Historic abstinence (General Rules); holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) still ask members to abstain; UMC recommends abstinence as a witness.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Occult forbidden; fantasy generally accepted.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Respect for other faiths; evangelism encouraged.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Varies; strong peace emphasis in UMC; revenge rejected.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Holiness and chastity; explicit content a concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: UMC affirming since 2024; Global Methodist, Wesleyan and Nazarene traditional.
topics.Gender roles and family: Women ordained across most Methodist bodies; egalitarian.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Respect authority; social holiness may challenge injustice.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Grace and assurance; suicide treated pastorally.

Methodist / Wesleyan.media: Wesley's General Rules ask members to avoid "diversions as cannot be used in the name of the Lord Jesus" and books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God." Holiness churches keep this caution; the United Methodist Church is much more open today.

Muslim.beliefs: There is one God (Allah), Creator of all, without partner (tawhid). Humans are created to worship God and act as stewards on earth; after death comes the Day of Judgment, then paradise or hell. Authority rests on the Qur'an as God's word, the Sunnah (example) of the Prophet Muhammad in hadith, and scholarly interpretation (fiqh) through the schools of law; Shia Muslims also follow the Imams and their marja'.
Muslim.values: The Five Pillars (declaration of faith, five daily prayers, zakat, Ramadan fasting, Hajj); taqwa (God-consciousness), honesty, modesty, kindness to parents, generosity, patience and justice.
Muslim.forbids: Shirk (associating partners with God), sorcery (sihr), alcohol and intoxicants, pork, gambling, sex outside marriage, immodest images, lying, backbiting and mockery of the sacred. Many scholars discourage music and depictions of living beings, to different degrees; depicting prophets is widely forbidden.
Muslim.family: Marriage (nikah) between a man and a woman is strongly encouraged; sex belongs within marriage; modest dress for men and women (hijab for women as most scholars teach); distinct complementary roles. Identity is marked by prayer, halal food, Ramadan and the two Eids, Arabic recitation and modest dress.
Muslim.stories: Storytelling with a moral purpose is valued (the Qur'an calls Joseph's story "the best of stories"). Fiction is judged by its content: magic shown as real power, prophets depicted, or immorality glamorized are common concerns.
Muslim.range: Sunni, Shia and diverse cultural practices; observance levels vary.
Muslim.sources: Qur'an and Hadith; fatwa councils (e.g. Fiqh Council of North America); Muslim parenting and media guides.

topics.Alcohol: Forbidden (Qur'an 5:90).
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Sihr (sorcery) forbidden; jinn are real in Islamic belief; magic shown positively is a concern.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Shirk (associating partners with God) is the gravest sin; multiple gods shown as real or worshipped is a concern.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Fighting only in just cause; mercy emphasized; revenge limited by law and forgiveness preferred.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Modesty (haya) for men and women; sexual content and fan service a significant concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Traditional teaching.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Blasphemy against God or prophets a serious concern; foul language discouraged.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Obedience to parents (Qur'an 17:23).
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Afterlife and judgment; suicide forbidden.
topics.Lying and deception: Lying forbidden, with narrow exceptions (reconciliation, war).

Muslim.media: Scholars differ on images of living beings; depicting prophets (including Jesus and Moses as prophets), God or angels is widely forbidden. Music is debated. "Lowering the gaze" (Qur'an 24:30-31) shapes views on immodest content, and some read 31:6 ("idle talk") as caution about entertainment.

Non-denominational Evangelical.beliefs: God created the world; humans are sinners saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection bring forgiveness. Believers will live with God forever; those who reject Christ face judgment. Authority rests on the Bible as inspired and without error, with each church's statement of faith and elders or pastors leading.
Non-denominational Evangelical.values: A personal relationship with Jesus ("born again"); Bible reading and prayer; evangelism and missions; contemporary worship; small groups; serving others.
Non-denominational Evangelical.forbids: Sexual immorality and pornography, drunkenness and drug abuse, occult involvement, profanity and taking God's name in vain, and media that celebrate sin.
Non-denominational Evangelical.family: Marriage between one man and one woman; sex within marriage; many churches teach complementary roles, others are egalitarian. Identity is marked by conversion and believer's baptism, church involvement, youth group and Christian music and media.
Non-denominational Evangelical.stories: Stories are judged by whether they honor God; many embrace fantasy (Narnia, Tolkien) while some avoid magic and occult themes. Reviews such as Plugged In are widely used.
Non-denominational Evangelical.range: Very broad: from conservative Bible churches to culturally progressive megachurches.
Non-denominational Evangelical.sources: Scripture; Lausanne Covenant; NAE statements; Plugged In (Focus on the Family); The Gospel Coalition; Christianity Today reviews.

topics.Alcohol: Varies; moderation common, some abstain; drunkenness condemned.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Occult practice forbidden; fantasy magic debated (many accept Tolkien/Lewis-style magic, are wary of spells and spirit contact).
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Exclusive claims of Christ; worldview of other religions discussed rather than banned.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Just war accepted; revenge rejected; graphic violence weighed by purpose.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Purity emphasis; sexual content and fan service a concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Traditional sexual ethics in most churches; some affirming congregations.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Honor parents; respect authority; rebellion against evil authority can be admired.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Salvation by faith; heaven and hell; suicide handled pastorally.
topics.Lying and deception: Lying sinful; discussion of motives encouraged.

Non-denominational Evangelical.media: Philippians 4:8 and Romans 14 (freedom and conscience) guide choices. Many distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it and speak of "engaging" or "redeeming" culture; others favor separation. Plugged In and Christianity Today reviews are common references.

Orthodox Jewish.beliefs: One God created the world and gave the Torah, written and oral, to Israel at Sinai. Orthodox Judaism centers on halakha (Jewish law) as binding and divinely given; the purpose of life is to serve God through the mitzvot (commandments), Torah study and refining one's character. Belief in reward and punishment, the coming of the Messiah, the world to come (olam haba) and resurrection of the dead (Maimonides' Thirteen Principles). Authority rests with the Torah, the Talmud, the codes and recognized rabbinic decisors (poskim). The focus is inward: on living the community's own law and learning tradition rather than on outside culture.
Orthodox Jewish.values: Torah study (talmud Torah) as a supreme value; Shabbat and holiday observance; kashrut; prayer; acts of loving-kindness (chesed) and charity (tzedakah); honoring parents; guarding one's speech.
Orthodox Jewish.forbids: Idolatry, sorcery and divination; desecrating Shabbat; forbidden foods; lashon hara (harmful speech) and nivul peh (vulgar speech); immodest images and sexual content; time-wasting entertainment that displaces Torah study (bittul Torah).
Orthodox Jewish.family: Marriage between a man and a woman is a central mitzvah; family purity laws govern marital relations; men and women have distinct ritual roles; tzniut (modesty) in dress and conduct. Identity is marked by brit milah, bar/bat mitzvah, kippah and tzitzit for men, covered hair for married women in most communities, kosher home and the Jewish calendar.
Orthodox Jewish.stories: Stories in the tradition are mainly Torah, midrash and tales of the sages; outside fiction is judged by halakhic concerns about speech, modesty and idolatry.
Orthodox Jewish.range: Modern Orthodox to Haredi (Hasidic and Litvish); communities follow their own rabbinic authorities (poskim). Many Haredi communities are strongly inward-focused.
Orthodox Jewish.sources: Torah and Talmud; Shulchan Aruch and Mishnah Berurah; rulings of recognized poskim; Orthodox Union and Agudath Israel guidance.

topics.Alcohol: Wine is part of ritual (Kiddush, Purim); drunkenness otherwise discouraged.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Drug abuse prohibited (guarding health, Deuteronomy 4:15); many poskim now prohibit smoking.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Sorcery and necromancy forbidden (Deuteronomy 18:10-11); Haredi families often avoid fantasy magic, Modern Orthodox families are more accepting.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Idolatry (avodah zarah) shown approvingly is a concern; antisemitic tropes a key concern.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Self-defense permitted; revenge forbidden (Leviticus 19:18).
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Strict modesty (tzniut); sexual content and immodest images a significant concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Same-sex acts forbidden (Leviticus 18:22); same-sex romance usually a significant concern.
topics.Gender roles and family: Distinct roles for men and women in ritual and family.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Vulgar speech (nivul peh) and harmful speech (lashon hara) avoided; misuse of God's name serious.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Honor parents (Exodus 20:12); respect for rabbinic authority.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: World to come and resurrection; suicide traditionally grave, with compassionate rulings in practice.

Orthodox Jewish.media: Lashon hara, nivul peh and tzniut govern what is watched and read. Many Haredi communities restrict secular media and the internet to protect the home and community; Modern Orthodox families are selective but engaged. Torah study is valued above entertainment.

Pentecostal / Charismatic.beliefs: God created the world; salvation through faith in Jesus Christ; believers are empowered by the baptism in the Holy Spirit, often evidenced by speaking in tongues, with spiritual gifts such as healing and prophecy active today. Christ will return; believers will live with God forever and the unsaved face judgment. Authority rests on the Bible, with the Spirit's guidance and pastoral leadership.
Pentecostal / Charismatic.values: Spirit-filled worship, prayer and fasting; healing; evangelism and missions; holiness of life; testimony.
Pentecostal / Charismatic.forbids: Witchcraft, occult practice and demonic involvement are taken very seriously; sexual immorality; drunkenness and drugs; profanity; worldliness (stricter holiness standards in some churches).
Pentecostal / Charismatic.family: Marriage between one man and one woman; sex within marriage; modesty; women preach in many churches (the Assemblies of God credentials women). Identity is marked by water baptism, Spirit baptism, lively worship and church community.
Pentecostal / Charismatic.stories: Because spiritual warfare is real in this view, many families are cautious about magic, demons and the occult in stories even when fictional; uplifting and faith-building media are preferred.
Pentecostal / Charismatic.range: Assemblies of God, Church of God in Christ, Foursquare, independent charismatic churches; holiness standards vary.
Pentecostal / Charismatic.sources: Assemblies of God "16 Fundamental Truths" and position papers; Church of God (Cleveland) practical commitments; Scripture.

topics.Alcohol: Many abstain (AG position paper on abstinence from alcohol).
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Spiritual warfare is central: demons, curses, spirit contact and occult imagery are often a significant concern even in fiction.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Other gods may be seen as spiritually real and dangerous; strong caution.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Varies; revenge rejected; graphic violence a concern.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Holiness and modesty emphasized; sexual content a significant concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Traditional teaching (AG position papers).
topics.Gender roles and family: Women may preach in many Pentecostal churches; family roles often traditional.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Honor parents; spiritual authority respected.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Heaven and hell vivid; suicide treated pastorally.

Pentecostal / Charismatic.media: Media can be an "open door" to spiritual influence, so occult and demonic content is weighed more heavily than in many traditions. Holiness standards (modesty, separation from worldliness) vary by church.

Reform Jewish.beliefs: One God, in covenant with the Jewish people; Torah is a foundational, evolving, human response to the divine, studied with modern scholarship. Ethical monotheism and the prophetic call to justice are central. Beliefs about the afterlife vary; the 1999 platform speaks of hope for redemption and a messianic age rather than a personal Messiah. Authority is personal autonomy informed by tradition, study and community, with guidance from the Central Conference of American Rabbis (CCAR).
Reform Jewish.values: Tikkun olam (social justice), Torah study, prayer, Shabbat and holidays as chosen practice, tzedakah, inclusion, Israel and Jewish peoplehood.
Reform Jewish.forbids: Few ritual prohibitions are treated as binding; ethical commandments are: no cruelty, deceit, exploitation or harmful speech. Antisemitic and hateful content is a key concern.
Reform Jewish.family: Full gender equality; LGBTQ people fully included and same-sex marriage celebrated; interfaith families welcomed and patrilineal descent recognized (1983). Identity is marked by naming and brit milah, bar/bat mitzvah, confirmation, Shabbat, holidays and congregational life.
Reform Jewish.stories: Fiction and the arts are embraced; content is judged by ethical values rather than ritual law.
Reform Jewish.range: Union for Reform Judaism and Central Conference of American Rabbis; personal autonomy informed by tradition.
Reform Jewish.sources: Pittsburgh Platform (1885); Columbus Platform (1937); "A Statement of Principles for Reform Judaism" (Pittsburgh, 1999); CCAR and URJ resolutions.

topics.Alcohol: Moderation; concern about addiction.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Fantasy accepted.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Interfaith respect; antisemitic tropes a key concern.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Tikkun olam and justice; concern about glorified violence.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Ethics of consent and healthy relationships.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Affirming (CCAR supports rabbis officiating same-sex marriages, 2000).
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Informed personal autonomy.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Diverse beliefs about afterlife.

Reform Jewish.media: No formal media rules. Informed autonomy, tikkun olam and attention to antisemitism and stereotypes guide choices.

Reformed / Presbyterian.beliefs: God is sovereign over all things and created the world for His glory; "man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever" (Westminster Shorter Catechism). Humans are fallen; God saves His elect by grace through faith in Christ alone. Believers rise to eternal life; the unbelieving to judgment. Authority rests on Scripture alone, summarized in the Westminster Standards or the Three Forms of Unity and governed by elders (presbyteries).
Reformed / Presbyterian.values: God's glory in all of life; preaching of the Word; covenant children and family worship; catechism; Lord's Day observance; vocation and cultural engagement.
Reformed / Presbyterian.forbids: The Ten Commandments as expounded in the catechisms, including idolatry and images of God (many Reformed hold that depicting Christ breaks the second commandment), blasphemy, Sabbath-breaking, sexual sin, and lying.
Reformed / Presbyterian.family: PCA, OPC and URC hold marriage between one man and one woman and ordain only men; PC(USA) ordains women and permits same-sex marriage. Identity is marked by infant baptism, profession of faith, catechism and Lord's Day worship.
Reformed / Presbyterian.stories: Common grace allows appreciation of good art by anyone; fiction is judged by its worldview and whether it portrays sin truthfully or attractively.
Reformed / Presbyterian.range: Conservative (PCA, OPC, URC) to mainline (PC(USA)); the Westminster Standards or Three Forms of Unity are the shared references in conservative churches.
Reformed / Presbyterian.sources: Westminster Confession and Catechisms; Heidelberg Catechism; Kuyper on common grace; Reformed media reviews (e.g. The Gospel Coalition, Ligonier).

topics.Alcohol: Moderate use permitted; drunkenness sinful (WLC Q139).
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Occult practice forbidden; fantasy judged through "common grace" and how it is framed.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Other religions as false worship; art by non-Christians still valued (common grace).
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Just war accepted; magistrate may bear the sword; revenge rejected.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Chastity; concern over sexual imagery (WLC Q139).
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Traditional teaching in conservative churches; PC(USA) is affirming.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Fifth commandment covers all authority (WLC Q123-133).
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Sovereignty of God, providence; suicide is self-murder (WLC Q136) but handled pastorally.

Reformed / Presbyterian.media: Common grace (Kuyper) lets families value good art by non-Christians. Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 lists "lascivious songs, books, pictures... stage plays" among sins against the seventh commandment. The second commandment (Heidelberg Catechism Q96-98) makes images of God or Christ a concern for many.

Satanist.beliefs: Both main organizations are non-theistic: Satan is a symbol, not a being to worship. The Church of Satan sees the human as an animal and each individual as their own god; there is no afterlife, so life should be lived fully now. The Satanic Temple uses Satan as a symbol of rebellion against arbitrary authority and of reason and compassion. Authority: for the Church of Satan, Anton LaVey's writings; for The Satanic Temple, its Seven Fundamental Tenets, with no claim to divine authority.
Satanist.values: Church of Satan: indulgence rather than abstinence, self-preservation, personal responsibility, individualism. The Satanic Temple: compassion and empathy, justice, bodily autonomy, freedom of others, scientific understanding, admitting and correcting mistakes, and pursuit of the noble.
Satanist.forbids: Church of Satan Eleven Rules: harming little children, killing non-human animals except for food or self-defense, and unwanted sexual advances; compulsive behavior. The Satanic Temple: encroaching on others' freedoms and acting against reason.
Satanist.family: Consenting adults are free in sexual matters; egalitarian and LGBTQ-affirming. Identity is marked by membership, ritual or community events, and in The Satanic Temple, activism for religious pluralism and separation of church and state.
Satanist.stories: Literature and art, including Milton's Satan as heroic rebel, are valued; occult imagery is aesthetic or psychodramatic; concern is mainly with stereotyped depictions of Satanists.
Satanist.range: Non-theistic Satanism: the Church of Satan (individualist, founded 1966) and The Satanic Temple (activist, founded 2013), which differ. Neither believes in a literal Satan. Theistic Satanists are small and have no central texts.
Satanist.sources: The Satanic Bible (Anton LaVey, 1969); Nine Satanic Statements; Eleven Satanic Rules of the Earth; The Satanic Temple's Seven Fundamental Tenets.

topics.Alcohol: Indulgence rather than compulsion (Church of Satan).
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Church of Satan discourages drug use (to verify); Satanic Temple stresses bodily autonomy (Tenet 3).
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Church of Satan treats ritual magic as psychodrama; not a concern in fiction.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Religious freedom and pluralism strongly valued; concern about religion imposed by authority and about "Satanic panic" stereotypes.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Church of Satan accepts proportionate retaliation; Satanic Temple emphasizes compassion and justice (Tenets 1 and 2).
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Consenting adults free; harm to children condemned (Eleven Rules).
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Affirming.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Rebellion against arbitrary authority admired.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: No afterlife; life lived now.
topics.Lying and deception: Satanic Temple: beliefs should follow the best scientific understanding (Tenet 5).

Satanist.media: No content code. Art that challenges authority is valued (Milton's Satan as heroic rebel). Concerns are harm to children and animals (Eleven Rules) and stereotyped depictions of Satanists.

Scientologist.beliefs: Each person is a thetan: an immortal spiritual being who has lived many lives and is basically good. The aim is spiritual freedom and full awareness, reached step by step along "the Bridge to Total Freedom." Existence is viewed through the eight dynamics, urges toward survival that run from self to family, groups, humankind, all life, the physical universe, spirit and the Supreme Being. Authority rests on the writings and lectures of L. Ron Hubbard, applied as written ("standard technology") by the Church of Scientology.
Scientologist.values: Auditing (spiritual counseling) and training; study technology; communication; personal integrity ("what is true for you is what you have observed yourself"); honesty; the ARC triangle (affinity, reality, communication); helping others and improving society.
Scientologist.forbids: The Way to Happiness precepts include not harming people of good will, not doing anything illegal, not murdering, not stealing, being trustworthy and taking care of oneself. The church opposes illegal drugs and campaigns against psychiatry and psychiatric drugs.
Scientologist.family: The second dynamic covers sex, family and raising children; Hubbard's code stresses faithfulness to one's sexual partner. Identity is marked by course and auditing progress, church services and naming ceremonies, and the church's community and humanitarian programs.
Scientologist.stories: Hubbard was a prolific fiction writer and praised the artist's role in society; there is no formal content code. Portrayals of psychiatry and of the church itself are areas of concern.
Scientologist.range: Church of Scientology International; independent ("Free Zone") Scientologists practice outside it.
Scientologist.sources: The Way to Happiness (L. Ron Hubbard, 1981); Creed of the Church of Scientology; Code of a Scientologist; Dianetics.

topics.Alcohol: Avoided around auditing; excess discouraged (The Way to Happiness).
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Strongly opposed to harmful drugs (The Way to Happiness); the Church opposes psychiatric drugs, so positive portrayals of psychiatry may be a concern.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Not a stated concern.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Creed affirms freedom of religion.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: "Do not murder" (The Way to Happiness); concern about glorified violence.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: "Be faithful to your sexual partner" (The Way to Happiness).
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Church states it does not discriminate (to verify).
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: "Honor and help your parents"; support for just government.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: The spirit (thetan) is immortal and lives many lives.
topics.Lying and deception: "Be worthy of trust"; "Seek to live with the truth."

Scientologist.media: No content code for fiction. The Way to Happiness precepts and the Church's opposition to psychiatry are the main lenses.

Secular humanist.beliefs: The universe is natural and knowable through science; humans are the product of evolution. There is no supernatural creator or afterlife, so meaning is made in this life. Authority rests on reason, evidence and shared human experience, not revelation.
Secular humanist.values: Critical thinking and inquiry; compassion and empathy; human rights and dignity; freedom of conscience; democracy; science education; personal responsibility and living ethically without religion.
Secular humanist.forbids: No formal prohibitions; harm, cruelty, dishonesty, coercion and dogmatism are rejected on ethical grounds. Pseudoscience presented as fact is a concern.
Secular humanist.family: Equality of the sexes; consenting relationships, including same-sex marriage, are affirmed; children are raised to think for themselves. Identity is marked loosely: humanist celebrations (naming ceremonies, weddings, memorials), Darwin Day, local humanist communities.
Secular humanist.stories: Fiction, including myths, gods and magic, is welcomed as imaginative and cultural; concern is with stories that present superstition as truth or celebrate cruelty.
Secular humanist.range: Non-religious families who stress reason, science and human flourishing.
Secular humanist.sources: Humanist Manifesto III (2003); American Humanist Association; AAP media guidance.

topics.Alcohol: Responsible use; age-appropriate concern.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Not a concern as fiction; concern about promoting pseudoscience as real.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Neutral; concern about religious coercion.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Concern about glorified violence; reason and empathy valued.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Concern about exploitation; consent emphasized.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Accepting.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Critical thinking about authority valued.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: This-life focus; mental-health framing on suicide.

Secular humanist.media: Free inquiry and opposition to censorship are valued, with critical thinking about what is shown. Concern centers on cruelty, exploitation and pseudoscience presented as fact.

Secular progressive.beliefs: This is a values frame rather than a religion: families who are generally non-religious and see society as improvable through inclusion, equality and collective action. Views on origins come from science; the afterlife is usually not part of the frame. Authority rests on human rights, evidence and the experience of affected communities.
Secular progressive.values: Equality and inclusion; diversity; empathy; social and environmental justice; consent; mental health; critical thinking about power and representation.
Secular progressive.forbids: No formal prohibitions; bigotry, racism, sexism, homophobia and transphobia, bullying, exploitation and harmful stereotypes are the main concerns in media.
Secular progressive.family: Many family forms are valued equally; LGBTQ identities affirmed; gender roles seen as flexible; emphasis on consent and body autonomy. Identity is marked by civic engagement, community and advocacy rather than ritual.
Secular progressive.stories: Fiction, myth and magic are welcomed; stories are judged by representation, who is centered, and how violence, gender and race are portrayed.
Secular progressive.range: Non-religious families who prioritize equality, inclusion and social justice.
Secular progressive.sources: Common Sense Media; American Academy of Pediatrics media guidance; diversity and representation reviews.

topics.Alcohol: Concern about glamorized drinking for minors.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Not a concern.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Values respectful, accurate portrayals of all faiths; concern about stereotypes.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Concern about glorified violence and militarism.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Concern about sexualization, especially of minors, and consent.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: LGBTQ representation welcomed; stereotypes or mockery a concern.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Slurs and demeaning language a concern more than mild profanity.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Questioning unjust authority valued.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Mental-health framing; concern about portrayals of suicide (safe-messaging guidelines).

Secular progressive.media: No religious rules. Judgments focus on representation, consent, stereotypes and age-appropriateness (Common Sense Media, AAP guidance).

Seventh-day Adventist.beliefs: God created the world in six literal days and rested on the seventh; humanity fell and is saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ. The dead sleep unconsciously until Christ's soon Second Coming, when the righteous are raised to eternal life; the wicked are ultimately destroyed rather than tormented forever. Authority rests on the Bible as the only rule of faith, with Ellen G. White's writings regarded as an inspired guide, under the General Conference.
Seventh-day Adventist.values: The seventh-day Sabbath (Friday sunset to Saturday sunset); health and wholeness of body, mind and spirit; education; mission and service; Bible study; simplicity.
Seventh-day Adventist.forbids: Alcohol, tobacco and drugs; unclean meats (many are vegetarian); spiritualism and occult practice; sexual immorality; media that degrade or excite the passions; secular entertainment on the Sabbath.
Seventh-day Adventist.family: Marriage between one man and one woman; modesty and simplicity in dress and adornment. Identity is marked by believer's baptism, Sabbath keeping, Adventist schools and Pathfinders, and health practices.
Seventh-day Adventist.stories: Ellen White warned against fiction that excites the imagination; today many members accept wholesome fiction while some still avoid it, and spiritualism or magic in stories is a common concern.
Seventh-day Adventist.range: Worldwide church under the General Conference; members range from conservative to progressive, especially on women's ordination and media.
Seventh-day Adventist.sources: 28 Fundamental Beliefs (esp. #22 Christian Behavior, #26 Death and Resurrection); writings of Ellen G. White; General Conference official statements; Adventist Review.

topics.Alcohol: Abstinence from alcohol is expected of members (health message, Fundamental Belief 22).
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Tobacco and recreational drugs not used; health message central.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Spiritualism strongly rejected; the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so ghosts or spirits of the dead shown as real are a particular concern.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Christ as Savior; other faiths respected; strong emphasis on Sabbath and end-time prophecy.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Historic noncombatant stance (many serve as medics); concern about glorified violence.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Chastity and modest dress; sexual content a concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Marriage between one man and one woman (General Conference statements); same-sex romance usually a significant concern.
topics.Gender roles and family: Strong family emphasis; women's ordination debated (2015 General Conference vote).
topics.Language and blasphemy: Clean, reverent speech; misuse of God's name a concern.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Respect for parents and lawful authority; conscience above state on Sabbath and worship.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Death is a sleep until the resurrection; no eternal torment; suicide met with pastoral care.

Seventh-day Adventist.media: Fundamental Belief 22 asks members to choose entertainment "of the highest quality" and avoid what is impure. Ellen White warned against fiction and theatre that excite the passions; "by beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) is a common principle.

Shinto.beliefs: The world is filled with kami: divine presences in nature, ancestors and places. The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki tell how the kami Izanagi and Izanami formed the islands of Japan. Shinto has no single founder, creed or scripture; it centers on ritual and on living in harmony with the kami. Death is a source of impurity; ancestors are honored as spirits, with afterlife beliefs often drawn from Buddhism. Authority rests with shrine tradition and priests, and for most shrines the Association of Shinto Shrines (Jinja Honchō).
Shinto.values: Purity (harae, purification), sincerity (makoto), gratitude, harmony with nature and community, respect for ancestors, festivals (matsuri) and seasonal rites.
Shinto.forbids: Pollution (kegare) through death, blood or wrongdoing; disrespect at shrines or to the kami; there is no list of commandments.
Shinto.family: Family and household continuity and ancestor veneration are central; weddings are often held in Shinto style. Identity is marked by shrine visits (Shichi-Go-San, New Year hatsumōde), home altars (kamidana), amulets and festivals; many Japanese practice it alongside Buddhism.
Shinto.stories: Kami, spirits (yōkai), magic and myth appear naturally in Japanese stories and anime; respectful portrayal of shrines and kami matters more than avoiding the supernatural.
