Shinto.range: Shrine Shinto (Association of Shinto Shrines), folk Shinto and sect Shinto; many Japanese practice it alongside Buddhism without an exclusive identity.
Shinto.sources: Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (myth); Association of Shinto Shrines, "Principles of Life in Reverence of Kami" (Keishin Seikatsu no Koryo); shrine practice.

topics.Alcohol: Sake is offered to kami (omiki) and drinking at festivals is normal.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: No specific teaching; social norms apply.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Kami, spirits and yokai are part of the worldview; the concern is disrespect toward kami or shrines.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Syncretic; coexists with Buddhism and other faiths.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: No pacifist doctrine; blood and death bring ritual impurity (kegare).
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: No codified sexual ethic; fertility festivals exist.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: No doctrine; shrine practice on same-sex ceremonies varies (to verify).
topics.Gender roles and family: Some traditional ritual roles; women have served as priests since 1946.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Reverence for ancestors, community and harmony.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Death is impure (kegare); funerals usually Buddhist; ancestors honored.

Shinto.media: No doctrine on fiction. Kami and yokai are common in Japanese popular culture and generally accepted. Concerns center on disrespect toward shrines and kami; sincerity, purity and gratitude are the values applied.

Sikh.beliefs: There is one God (Ik Onkar), the formless Creator, present in all creation. Humans pass through cycles of birth and death by karma; the goal is liberation (mukti) through God's grace by remembering God's Name (Naam) and overcoming ego (haumai). Authority rests on the Guru Granth Sahib, the eternal living Guru, and the Khalsa Panth; the Akal Takht issues the Sikh Rehat Maryada (code of conduct).
Sikh.values: Naam japna (remembering God), kirat karni (honest work) and vand chakna (sharing); seva (selfless service); langar (free community kitchen); equality of all people; courage to defend the oppressed.
Sikh.forbids: For initiated Sikhs, the four kurehits: cutting hair, eating ritually slaughtered (halal/kutha) meat, adultery, and tobacco. Alcohol and drugs, superstition, idol worship and caste discrimination are rejected.
Sikh.family: Marriage (Anand Karaj) is a spiritual union; equality of men and women; modesty. Identity is marked by the Five Ks for the initiated (kesh, kara, kanga, kachera, kirpan), the turban (dastaar), the names Singh and Kaur, amrit initiation and the gurdwara.
Sikh.stories: Sakhis (stories of the Gurus) and martyrdom history are central; depicting the Gurus by actors is widely rejected, and the Akal Takht has objected to animated or acted portrayals. Disrespect to the turban, kirpan or Guru Granth Sahib is a key concern.
Sikh.range: Amritdhari (initiated) to Sahajdhari and diaspora families; observance varies.
Sikh.sources: Guru Granth Sahib; Sikh Rehat Maryada (code of conduct, SGPC); teachings of the ten Gurus; Akal Takht edicts.

topics.Alcohol: Forbidden for initiated Sikhs and widely discouraged.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Tobacco strictly forbidden (one of four kurahits); intoxicants forbidden.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Magic, superstition and astrology rejected by the Gurus.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: One God; respect for all paths; mockery of the Gurus or Sikh symbols a significant concern.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Defending the oppressed is righteous (Guru Gobind Singh); vengeance for personal gain rejected.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Sex only within marriage; adultery a kurahit; modesty valued.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Akal Takht opposed same-sex marriage (2005); diaspora views vary.
topics.Gender roles and family: Equality of women and men taught by Guru Nanak.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Respectful speech; disrespect to kesh (uncut hair) or turbans a concern.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Respect for elders and the Guru.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Rebirth and liberation; acceptance of God's will (hukam); suicide discouraged.

Sikh.media: The Rehat Maryada does not address fiction. Depicting the Gurus in images or film is opposed by the SGPC. The five vices (lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego) shown as admirable are a concern.

Unitarian Universalist.beliefs: No required creed; members draw on many sources, including direct experience, world religions, Jewish and Christian teaching, humanism, science and earth-centered traditions. Views on God and afterlife range from theist to atheist; historically, Universalists taught that all are saved. Authority rests with individual conscience and the democratic congregation.
Unitarian Universalist.values: As revised in the UUA bylaws (2024), love at the center, with the shared values of interdependence, equity, transformation, pluralism, generosity and justice; earlier the Seven Principles, including the inherent worth and dignity of every person and a free and responsible search for truth and meaning.
Unitarian Universalist.forbids: No religious prohibitions; oppression, cruelty and discrimination are opposed on moral grounds.
Unitarian Universalist.family: LGBTQ people fully welcomed (Welcoming Congregation program); same-sex marriage celebrated; Our Whole Lives comprehensive sexuality education for children and youth. Identity is marked by congregational life, the flaming chalice symbol, child dedications, coming-of-age programs and social action.
Unitarian Universalist.stories: Stories from many religions and cultures are taught; fiction, myth and magic are welcomed, with concern for cruelty, bigotry and exclusion.
Unitarian Universalist.range: Unitarian Universalist Association congregations; members include humanists, theists, pagans, Buddhists and others.
Unitarian Universalist.sources: UUA Principles and Sources (Seven Principles, proposed Eighth Principle); 2024 revision of UUA Article II (Love with six values: interdependence, pluralism, justice, transformation, generosity, equity); Our Whole Lives (OWL) sexuality curriculum.

topics.Alcohol: Personal choice; concern about addiction and glamorizing for minors.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Not a concern as fiction; pagan members (CUUPS) value respectful portrayals.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Pluralism valued; concern about disrespect toward any faith.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Peace and justice emphasis; concern about glorified violence.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Age-appropriate, consent-based sexuality education (OWL); concern about exploitation.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Affirming (Welcoming Congregation program); concern about negative LGBTQ portrayals.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Not a major concern; slurs and demeaning speech are.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Free and responsible search for truth; questioning authority valued.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Beliefs about afterlife vary widely.

Unitarian Universalist.media: No formal media rules. The principles (inherent worth and dignity, justice, free search for truth) are applied, with concern about stereotypes and attention to age-appropriateness.

Wiccan / Pagan.beliefs: The divine is present in nature, often honored as a Goddess and God or many deities. Life follows the seasonal Wheel of the Year; many Wiccans believe in reincarnation and a restful otherworld (the Summerland). There is no central scripture or authority; covens, traditions and individual experience guide practice.
Wiccan / Pagan.values: Reverence for nature; personal responsibility; balance; the eight sabbats and moon rituals (esbats); magic understood as focusing will and energy; freedom of practice.
Wiccan / Pagan.forbids: The Wiccan Rede: "An it harm none, do what ye will"; many also hold the Threefold Law (what you send out returns). Harmful or manipulative magic is rejected.
Wiccan / Pagan.family: Sexuality is sacred and positive among consenting adults; most traditions are LGBTQ-affirming; handfasting as marriage. Identity is marked by initiation or self-dedication, the pentacle, sabbats and wiccanings (child blessings).
Wiccan / Pagan.stories: Myth, magic and other gods are welcome in stories; concern is with portrayals of witches and pagans as evil or Satanic.
Wiccan / Pagan.range: Wicca (Gardnerian, Alexandrian, eclectic), Druidry, Heathenry and eclectic paganism; no central authority.
Wiccan / Pagan.sources: The Wiccan Rede ("An it harm none, do what ye will"); Threefold Law; Charge of the Goddess (Doreen Valiente); Covenant of the Goddess; Pagan Federation.

topics.Alcohol: Used in some rituals (cakes and ale); moderation.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Magic is a real religious practice; the concern is misrepresentation (witches as evil or Satanic) and magic used to harm.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Polytheistic and pluralistic; concern about demonizing pagan gods.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: "Harm none"; self-defense accepted; Heathenry honors warrior virtues.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Sex seen as sacred between consenting adults (Charge of the Goddess); concern about exploitation.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Largely affirming.
topics.Gender roles and family: Divine feminine and masculine honored; some traditions keep gendered ritual roles.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Personal responsibility and autonomy valued.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Many hold reincarnation or the Summerland; death part of the wheel of the year.
topics.Lying and deception: Honor and keeping one's word valued.

Wiccan / Pagan.media: No central rule. The Rede ("harm none") guides choices, and the main concern is accurate, respectful portrayals of witches and pagans.

20th-century-boys.weigh: a false messiah and his cult are framed as evil and exposed; staged miracles and a staged resurrection are shown as frauds; the Pope and a Catholic priest are shown sympathetically (to verify on the page); repentance and atonement are open to many characters, including former cult members; violence is moderate and the climax turns on an apology and on refusing to kill innocents; scholars read the overall stance as secular and wary of all messiahs, including the heroes (Thomas 2012; Bancha 2020).

checklist.text: Confirm the Viz rating on vol. 1 (Teen Plus) and on the Perfect Edition (Older Teen per Otaku USA). Affects Series facts.
V1 (ch. 1-10): Donkey's death and how the staged suicide is drawn. Affects Mental health (5).
V1-4: cult rituals, smiles, "banishment," and Friend's staged levitation; find the chapter. Affects Religion theme and the Aum discussion.
V5 (ch. 44-54) and v8: Bloody New Year's Eve, Kenji's apparent death, virus deaths on the page. Affects Violence (6) and Fear (7).
V8-10: Friend Land, the Virtual World, Kyoko's near-suicide. Affects Mental health and Authoritarianism lens.
V9-11: Kanna in the mafia casino, guns, the "Love and Peace" drug offer; red-light and cross-dressing scenes. Affects Substances, Sexuality and Imitable behavior.

V13-15: Kiriko's backstory and how Kanna's conception is shown; the abandoned hospital note; the Pope's visit, the staged assassination, Friend's return, ch. 169 "hailed as a God." Confirm how the Pope, Father Nitani and the church are portrayed. Affects Religion theme and all Christian frame rows.
V16-18: world after the pandemic, exile of the unvaccinated, the Wall, the fake alien threat; ch. 203 "What would Fukubei do?" Affects Politics theme.
V19-22: Kenji's return, Maruo's bomb, Sadakiyo's knife at the Expo, Prisoner 13. Affects Violence and Mental health.
21st Century Boys v1-2 and the kanzenban ending: Friend's identity, Kenji's apology, the school-roof scene and any suicide imagery. Affects Mental health and the essay.
Check whether the cult uses any Buddhist, Hindu or Christian vocabulary or imagery (affects Dharmic lens, Buddhist row and the Aum parallel).
Spot-check Viz profanity in 3-4 chapters. Affects Language (4).
Read Urasawa's afterwords and any Nagasaki notes in the volumes and Perfect Edition; record any statement on Aum, religion or intent. Affects Creator context.
Open the CBR, Polygon, Fandom Post and Mangabookshelf pieces; look for any Christian or conservative review. Affects How readers took it.
Re-score and sign off: update the scores, change the label to Full read, record the reviewer, delete the photos.

akira.weigh: tyranny, secret experiments on children and drug control are framed as evil and end in catastrophe; a drugged cult that worships a child as emperor is exposed; a temple seer and a spirit medium are sympathetic and decisive; the teenage hero is crude and sexually exploitative early (Loveridge; Thompson) and matures without any reckoning tied to faith; the ending is cosmic transcendence plus a self-governing community; there is no clear God or moral law in the story. On the page: extreme violence (9), drugs (8), sexual exploitation and attempted rape involving teen characters.

alice-in-borderland.weigh: the story's message is a choice of life over despair, carried by sacrifice and love; cruelty, predation and the Beach's hedonism are condemned; there is no God-denial, and the setting implies an afterlife (the Joker is "neither God nor Devil"). Against that, it is extremely violent, it shows suicide and self-harm, and it includes two attempted sexual assaults on a high-school girl (ch. 20, 39) and sexual relationships involving high-school characters (ch. 10, 44), which is why it carries a content warning.

all-you-need-is-kill.weigh: war against an inhuman enemy framed as necessary and tragic, not glorious (Weber); perseverance and growth; sacrificial love (Rita and Keiji each give up life or love for humanity); a suicide-by-gunshot loop test played partly for laughs; the hero killing the woman he loves at her own proposal; no faith or afterlife. billy-bat.weigh: Jesus appears as a character who heals and who, asked by Judas what God looks like, draws the bat (ch. 14-17, vol. 2); the series presents a morally ambiguous entity, called "God/Devil" by fans, as a hidden guide behind Christianity and much of history; Francis Xavier is a carrier of its message; the entity speaks to chosen people, which some traditions read as spiritism; the series condemns murder, racism, Nazism and terror and treats protecting the innocent as heroic; how the Judas and Jesus scenes are actually framed on the page (reverent, neutral or revisionist) has not been confirmed and is the first item on the review checklist. One fan wiki summary (not yet matched by a second source) says Jesus tells Judas before his death that the bat is not the shape of God and that he drew only what was in Judas's mind, and that the bat then admits it deceived Judas. If the page confirms this, the story keeps Jesus distinct from the bat and casts the bat as a deceiver, and several Christian grades below would likely rise by one step; no grade has been moved on a single source. Also weighed: the man Hitler sends to spread the bat, who becomes the fake Chuck Culkin, is identified as Jewish (Japanese Wikipedia; TV Tropes, ch. 100), and in vol. 18 (likely) Middle East terrorists enforcing a ban on images cut off Yamagata's arms (Japanese Wikipedia).

black-butler.weigh: child abuse, trafficking and the cult are framed as evil; but the hero is bound to a demon by a pact he chooses and never repents of, revenge is his purpose, he rejects God, the demon is drawn as elegant and admired, and no path of forgiveness or redemption is offered so far (the series is ongoing). On the page: oblique sexual assault of children (ch. 135-136, the content-warning scene), suggestive framing of a 13-year-old, a child-trafficking auction, ritual murder of a child, frequent violence.

blame.weigh: the series never endorses cruelty, and the hostile system and Silicon Life are framed as threats; the protagonists protect humans; there is no religious content to mock or affirm; minds are copied and moved between bodies as if the self were data; the saving child is made from two women's genes; the ending is bittersweet but hopeful; and the gore and body horror are constant.

bleach.weigh: villains who seek to overthrow "god" (Aizen, Yhwach) are framed as evil and defeated; the heroes' own institution has done grave wrongs (Quincy extermination, ch. 46; human experiments, ch. 124) that are acknowledged but not fully judged; the afterlife is a Japanese-styled bureaucracy with Hell and reincarnation; the supreme being is a sealed, limbless puppet kept alive by sacrifice (ch. 615-621); Christian and Jewish sacred names and symbols (crosses, a communion-like rite, the Tetragrammaton as a villain's name) are used as costume for the antagonists; Nazi-style aesthetics are used for an invading army. On the page: constant sword violence (8), fear (7), mild fan service (4).

bloom-into-you.weigh: the series endorses a same-sex romance between teenage girls as its central good, including a first sexual encounter before marriage (ch. 44) and a lasting relationship (ch. 45); its other messages (honesty, being oneself, letting grief heal, kindness in rejection) are widely shared values. Traditions that hold marriage as between a man and a woman and sex within marriage will find the central message in conflict; traditions that affirm same-sex relationships will mostly weigh consent (Touko's kisses) and the aro/ace debate. No tradition's own documents were found commenting on this series.

blue-flag.weigh: the story's clearest messages are honesty, self-acceptance and rejecting cruelty, exposure and gossip, which nearly every tradition shares; it presents same-sex attraction as a normal part of some people's lives and its epilogue presents the adult Taichi and Toma as a married couple, a good outcome; no sexual content is reported. Unlike stories where a same-sex romance is consummated on the page, the conflict here is with the story's framing and ending rather than with depicted acts.

talking.Lutheran: Worth earned by works versus worth given by grace. What happens to the players who are cut?
talking.Methodist / Wesleyan: Growing toward "perfect love" versus growing toward perfect ego. Can holiness include fierce competition?
talking.Anglican / Episcopal: C.S. Lewis on pride as "the great sin" (Mere Christianity) set beside Ego's speeches.
talking.Anabaptist (Mennonite, Amish, Brethren): Gelassenheit (yieldedness) set beside "ego." Is there a way to excel that serves the community?
talking.Latter-day Saint: Righteous ambition versus pride. How would Isagi's goals change if they included lifting others?
talking.Mainline progressive Protestant: Who pays for a "winner takes all" system? What would justice for the eliminated players look like?
talking.Seventh-day Adventist: What does the story train us to admire? Compare Ego's program with the Adventist emphasis on balanced, cooperative living.
talking.Jehovah's Witness: Galatians 5:26 beside the program's rule that only one striker matters. Can sport be enjoyed without the competitive spirit?
talking.Christian Science: Is confidence rooted in personal ego or in a right understanding of one's spiritual identity?
talking.Orthodox Jewish: Can the yetzer hara of ambition be harnessed for good? Pirkei Avot 4:1 versus "devour your rivals."
talking.Conservative Jewish: When is ambition holy? The difference between striving and stepping on others.
talking.Reform Jewish: The individual and the community in Jewish ethics: Hillel's "If I am not for myself, who will be for me? If I am only for myself, what am I?" (Pirkei Avot 1:14).
talking.Muslim: Ihsan (excellence) versus kibr (arrogance). Is there a way to be a confident athlete with humility before God?
talking.Hindu: Arjuna's duty without attachment versus Isagi's hunger to win. Can one give full effort without ego?
talking.Buddhist: Does Isagi's suffering come from craving to be the best? What would right effort without self-grasping look like in sport?
talking.Sikh: Haumai and seva: could a striker serve the team? Compare Ego's creed with the Sikh call to overcome ego.
talking.Bahá'í: Competition versus cooperation in the Bahá'í writings. What would a "unity" version of Blue Lock look like?
talking.Shinto: Wa versus the lone striker. Can sincere individual effort serve the community?
talking.Wiccan / Pagan: Personal power and responsibility: is Ego's program "harming none"?
talking.Scientologist: Balancing the first dynamic (self) with the third (groups): a team as a "group dynamic."
talking.Secular progressive: Who designs a system where losers are "trash"? What would healthy competition look like (AAP guidance on youth sports)?
talking.Secular humanist: Is Ego's method rational or just harsh? Evidence on what actually builds great athletes.
talking.Conservative / traditional: Duty to one's country and team versus self-assertion. Is ambition a virtue when it serves the nation?
talking.Unitarian Universalist: The first principle (inherent worth and dignity) and the eliminated players.
talking.Satanist: Self-interest versus cruelty: the Church of Satan's distinction between indulgence and harming others. TST's first tenet on compassion beside Ego's program.

bungo-stray-dogs.weigh: a strong theme of redemption, mercy and belonging (former killers become protectors); evil framed as evil, but villains written to be understandable; the Port Mafia's boss and gangsters are given glamour; a villain who uses the language of sin and God; and, above all, suicide used again and again as a joke. On the page: moderate-to-strong violence (7), suicide talk and attempts (8), mild innuendo, a comic running gag about Mori's attraction to young girls, and no nudity reported.

chained-soldier.weigh: the monsters and the bureau's experiments are framed as evil; loyalty, service and family devotion are praised; but sexual contact outside any commitment is the story's built-in reward, framed as earned, comic and good, with BDSM-style dominance as a power source and a harem of competing women. That framing, not just the amount, is what lowers grades for traditions whose sexual ethics tie intimacy to marriage. An 11-year-old character gives cheek-kiss "rewards" (ch. 25). On the page: Yen Press 18+ rating, frequent nudity, moderate monster violence.

On the page: extreme gore and torture, several suicides, sexual-abuse backstories and fan service involving minors.

fire-punch.weigh: revenge shown as self-destroying (Agni kills Doma and children, then attempts suicide); slavery, trafficking and rape condemned through villains but used heavily as backdrop; an incestuous wish (ch. 1) and a later romance with a sister look-alike; a man made into a false god, with religion shown as human invention; a sympathetic trans man (Togata); a bleak cosmic ending with a quiet note of peace. On the page: violence 10, sexual violence 9, self-harm 10.

food-wars.weigh: the core story praises hard work, humility, serving others and resisting an abusive father and a controlling regime; there is almost no violence or religion. The message question for many traditions is that the sexualized reactions of teenage characters are played as harmless comedy throughout, which is endorsement by tone rather than mere depiction; the epilogue adds a half-sibling marriage plot that the story does not frame as wrong before it ends (Le dessert). On the page: frequent fan service with covered nudity (6), mild language, no gore.

fullmetal-alchemist.weigh: the story punishes "playing God" (human transmutation, Father's absorption of God, ch. 104-108) and rewards humility; a fake religion is exposed (ch. 1-2) while a sincere persecuted faith (Ishvala) is honored; "Truth" is a non-Christian, pantheistic-sounding god figure; souls are bound to armor and Stones; genocide is condemned and its perpetrators seek atonement; the hero's skepticism about God is not overturned. given.weigh: the series endorses same-sex romance as its central good, both for high-school couples and adult couples. It shows adult premarital and casual sex mostly by implication, and it condemns a forced sexual advance. Its other messages are widely shared: grieving honestly, not living for one person to the point of codependency, perseverance, loyal friendship and forgiveness. No tradition's own documents were found commenting on this series.

gto-great-teacher-onizuka.weigh: the story affirms self-giving care for the outcast, rescue from suicide and reconciliation of families; it treats the hero's violence and rule-breaking as admirable; it plays a teacher's lust toward students and other sexual material for comedy, while abuse and rape appear in backstories framed as harm; authority is mostly shown as corrupt or self-serving. On the page: a 16+ title with constant sexual humor around minors, several suicide attempts and frequent comic violence.

horimiya.weigh: the story's core message (kindness, acceptance, loyalty, apology) is warm and clear; **teen premarital sex (ch. 37) is presented as a natural, loving step and is not judged**, though the couple later move toward engagement and marriage; Hori's violence toward Miyamura is sometimes condemned on the page (ch. 42) and sometimes a gag, and she enjoys him acting "mean" (ch. 43); Miyamura's self-harm and suicidal thoughts are in the past and are overcome through friendship, not therapy or faith; religion is nearly absent. On the page: sex is off-panel, there is kissing and shirtless art, mild language.

In this story Christ rises, then later dies in a distant land (ch. 67), which conflicts with the Ascension as most Christian churches teach it. On the page: frequent graphic gunfights and body horror (8), sexual threats against a 14-year-old (4), strong language.

komi-cant-communicate.weigh: the core message (patience with a struggling person, reaching out, friendship, a chaste and honest romance) is clear and warm; **no sex between the leads is reported**; fan-service gags and camera angles on schoolgirls (Common Sense Media) are the main depiction issue; **Najimi's undefined gender** is a point of concern for traditions with fixed teaching on sex and gender (cross-dressing, Deuteronomy 22:5 for some) and a point of welcome or of criticism for affirming frames, which split between "representation" and "stereotype"; Yamai's same-sex obsession is shown as unhealthy but comic and quickly forgiven; anxiety is overcome through friendship rather than faith or therapy.

my-lesbian-experience-with-loneliness.weigh: the book's main message (recovery from depression, self-worth, honesty, not living only for approval) is widely shared. Its premise, a paid same-sex sexual encounter outside marriage shown sympathetically though not as the answer, is where traditions divide. The author's own later view, that paying for affection could not give her the relationship she wanted (Bunshun), supports reading the encounter as not endorsed as a solution. No tradition's own documents were found commenting on this book.

nana.weigh: sex outside marriage is normal throughout and rarely questioned, though adultery and betrayal bring real pain; a planned abortion is set aside and the child is kept (ch. 25-29); heroin brings addiction and death (ch. 77); an adult's sexual relationship with a 15-year-old is shown (Shin and Reira); a controlling husband is not clearly judged by the story (the hiatus leaves this open); friendship, loyalty and forgiveness are the story's highest goods; there is no religious frame.

neon-genesis-evangelion.weigh: the message chooses life with others over escape, despair and forced merger, and the god-making plans of Seele and Gendo fail; adults who exploit children are shown as wrong; a dying father repents in part (stage 92). The sacred is treated as imagery: Angels are monstrous enemies, Lilith and Adam are giant beings, the Spear of Longinus is a weapon, crosses are visual motifs, and staff called the symbols decorative (Forward). No God figure appears. On the page: frequent and sometimes graphic violence (Toji's death, stages 39-40), several suicides and self-sacrifices, nudity of a 14-year-old girl (stage 14), a 14-year-old girl undressing in front of an adult who turns her down (stage 36) and an unwanted kiss between two boys (stage 67).

nisekoi.weigh: the message centers on kindness, honesty, loyalty and a single faithful choice that ends in marriage (ch. 227, 229), and a fake relationship that becomes real love; the concerns are organized crime shown as warm and comic with guns as gags, a teen deception of parents as the premise, slapstick violence by a girl toward a boy, a harem framing of several girls as rivals, and occasional fan service of high school characters (ch. 22-23, 44; anime OVAs). There is almost no religious content.

pandora-hearts.weigh: Jack's possessive love and Isla Yura's cult are framed as evil and fail; forgiveness and atonement are possible (Vincent, Oswald); Oz's self-acceptance is the core message; power comes from blood-sealed contracts with monsters, and illegal contracts are shown as corrupting; souls, an underworld and reincarnation are real in the story; Alice's suicide (ch. 78) is framed as a sacrifice; Oz's final self-giving is heroic. On the page: beheadings and gore, a suicide, child exploitation, little sexual content.

record-of-ragnarok.weigh: (1) Shiva and 12 other Hindu deities as tournament fighters and spectators (ch. 34-41, likely), with a documented objection from the Universal Society of Hinduism; (2) Buddha as a swaggering, lollipop-eating god who threatens other gods and wields a hatred-powered scythe (ch. 43-53); (3) Jesus as a silent spectator listed with Socrates and Confucius as one of the "sages" (ch. 46), cut from the anime; (4) Adam and Eve with a retold Eden where the Serpent attempts assault and the gods punish the innocent (Round 2, ch. 7-12); (5) Beelzebub, called "Satan" by VIZ's blurb, as a tragic god, with Satan, Lucifer and Lilith in his backstory (Round 8); (6) the gods as a body condemning humanity and humanity's defiance framed as heroic; (7) no Islamic figures and no Abrahamic God are shown.

rent-a-girlfriend.weigh: on the plus side, a self-giving love (the film made for a dying grandmother, ch. 102-167), care for elders, a hero who grows and apologizes, and an unresolved but chaste-leaning romance between adults. On the other side, the premise is paid companionship. A lie to sick grandparents and parents is kept up for hundreds of chapters, is partly justified (ch. 150) and is exposed late (after ch. 231). Lust and masturbation are played for comedy, there is an explicit sexual fantasy (ch. 218), and fan service is frequent. Faith content is almost nil.

shikimoris-not-just-a-cutie.weigh: the core message (a faithful, mutually protective couple who talk honestly, with warm families and good friends) is clear and gentle; **no sex, nudity or sexual dialogue is reported**; the depiction issues are mild (Izumi's admiration of his girlfriend, a beach trip and lakeside visit, a cheek kiss, a later kiss); the message issues are the **swap of gender roles** (welcomed by progressive readers, a talking point for complementarian ones), **teen dating** itself, a **first overnight trip as an unmarried couple at 18** that the publisher markets with innuendo though fans report nothing sexual happens (v20, ch. 175-176), and an **epilogue in which the couple, at university, plan to live together** (TV Tropes; MyAnimeList discussion; framing to verify). With the overnight trip and the cohabitation plan now reported by more than one source, grades for traditions that teach against cohabitation before marriage (Catholic, Baptist, Latter-day Saint, Bahá'í) move from A to B.

talking.Reform Jewish: Finding meaningful work. Memory as a blessing.
talking.Muslim: "To Allah we belong and to Him we return" (Qur'an 2:156) compared with Meiko's grief.
talking.Hindu: Gita on doing one's work without attachment to results.

talking.Unitarian Universalist: How each character searches for meaning.
talking.Satanist: Choosing your own path versus duty to others.

talking.Catholic: Inter Mirifica 7: is evil "made attractive," and is the fan service? The motto "a sound soul dwells in a sound mind and a sound body" and the body-soul unity. Crona's penance compared with repentance.
talking.Eastern Orthodox: Guarding the eyes and thoughts against the "madness" the story describes. Death as an enemy defeated by Christ versus Death as headmaster.
talking.Baptist: Philippians 4:8 as the test for prologues 1-3 and ch. 73-75. Is fear defeated by courage alone, or by trust in God (2 Timothy 1:7)?
talking.Non-denominational Evangelical: Romans 14 freedom versus causing others to stumble. Compare Maka's "courage" with "perfect love casts out fear" (1 John 4:18).
talking.Pentecostal / Charismatic: Ephesians 6:12 compared with the story's fantasy wars. Why might the church avoid stories that make witchcraft and death gods friendly?
talking.Reformed / Presbyterian: Is Justin's line about choosing gods true of people? Sovereignty of God compared with Death's flawed "absolute order" (ch. 108).
talking.Lutheran: Conscience and adiaphora: what in this series is "neither commanded nor forbidden," and what is not?
talking.Methodist / Wesleyan: Does this diversion "tend to the knowledge or love of God"? What does the Book of Eibon teach about each sin?
talking.Anglican / Episcopal: Lewis's Screwtape and the seven deadly sins compared with the Book of Eibon. What is the story's "god," and is he good?
talking.Anabaptist (Mennonite, Amish, Brethren): What would a nonviolent answer to Asura look like? Kid's truce as a peace witness.
talking.Latter-day Saint: Does the media invite the Spirit? The motto compared with the body as a temple.
talking.Mainline progressive Protestant: Who was treated as the enemy, and why did that end? How does the series treat Crona's abuse?
talking.Seventh-day Adventist: "By beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18) applied to the fan service and madness imagery. Fundamental Belief 22. (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Jehovah's Witness: jw.org's question: does it feature what God hates, especially spiritism and violence? (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Christian Science: "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392): Maka's victory over fear compared with denying fear's power. (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Orthodox Jewish: Lashon hara and nivul peh applied to the crude humor. The angel of death as God's servant compared with Death as an independent god. (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Conservative Jewish: Ending an old war with the witches: what makes reconciliation possible? (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Reform Jewish: Informed autonomy: what does a family choose to read and why? The witch hunt as a picture of scapegoating. (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Muslim: Who holds power over death in Islam, and how does the story's Death differ? Sihr in the Qur'an (2:102) compared with the story's witches.
talking.Hindu: Death as a keeper of order (Yama) compared with Lord Death. What does the Gita say about fear?
talking.Buddhist: Asura's fear compared with craving and aversion. Crona's choice to bear Asura (ch. 112): compassion or self-punishment?
talking.Sikh: Black☆Star's ego (haumai) and his humbling by Mifune (ch. 28-31). (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Bahá'í: Can a reconciliation like Kid's truce happen without justice first? (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Shinto: Purity of soul (a "sound soul") compared with harae (purification). (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Wiccan / Pagan: The arc from "witches are evil" to a truce. Harm none compared with the soul-hunt. (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Scientologist: Which Way to Happiness precepts does Maka live out? (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Secular progressive: Anime Feminist's argument that fan service undermines the partners' trust. Common Sense Media's 15+ rating.
talking.Secular humanist: Is the end of the Great Old Ones a humanist moment? What is "madness" in real life, and how is it different from the story's?
talking.Conservative / traditional: The good, the true and the beautiful: does the series show all three? Order versus "absolute order" (ch. 108).
talking.Unitarian Universalist: Can you honor someone's worth while fighting them? (from general knowledge; to verify)
talking.Satanist: Is Kid's new reign a break from Death's order, or more of the same? Compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1-2). (from general knowledge; to verify)

soul-eater.weigh: courage defeats fear and madness, and evil (Asura, Medusa, Arachne) is framed as evil; Crona's atonement and Maka's mercy offer redemption; Death personified as a god of order is the benevolent authority, but his flaw created the villain (ch. 108); souls are harvested and eaten; witches use real magic and the story ends the witch hunt (ch. 113); a priest figure turns to the villain (ch. 86); fan service, including of minors, is played as comedy (prologues 1-3, ch. 73-75, 113). On the page: violence 7, fear 7, sexuality 6, mental health 7.

talking.Catholic: Inter Mirifica 7: evil may be shown when it serves understanding and is not made attractive. Catechism on lying (CCC 2482-2486), drunkenness (CCC 2290), just war and self-defense (CCC 2263-2265, 2309). "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9).
talking.Eastern Orthodox: Theosis as growth in love: are Loid and Yor changed by love? The Fathers' debate on deception for another's good.
talking.Baptist: Philippians 4:8 as the common test; local-church autonomy and individual conscience mean standards vary; SBC resolutions urge abstinence from alcohol. Plugged In, widely used by Baptists, rates the manga 10+.
talking.Non-denominational Evangelical: Plugged In's TV and manga reviews as a discussion tool; Romans 14 on conscience. Ephesians 4:25 on truth; discuss the motives behind the lies.
talking.Pentecostal / Charismatic: Assemblies of God position on abstinence from alcohol; discernment about whether Anya's power is shown as spiritual or scientific.
talking.Reformed / Presbyterian: Kuyper on common grace in culture. Westminster Larger Catechism on the ninth commandment (Q144-145) and on drunkenness (Q139).
talking.Lutheran: Entertainment as adiaphora, judged by love and conscience. Law and gospel: the characters' failures and the grace they show each other. Eighth commandment: "put the best construction on everything."
talking.Methodist / Wesleyan: Prevenient grace at work in imperfect people; Wesley's General Rules ("do no harm"); social holiness and opposition to war. Holiness churches stricter than the UMC.
talking.Anglican / Episcopal: The Lewis and Sayers tradition of judging stories by how they frame good and evil; Book of Common Prayer marriage vows as a contrast to a contract marriage; Article 37 on just war.
talking.Anabaptist (Mennonite, Amish, Brethren): Nonresistance (Matthew 5:39); Schleitheim Confession, Article 4, on separation from the world. Discuss whether a story can oppose war while celebrating fighters. Mennonite Church USA families may be more open.
talking.Latter-day Saint: For the Strength of Youth (2022) on choosing media that invites the Spirit; "The Family: A Proclamation to the World" on the home as central.
talking.Seventh-day Adventist: Fundamental Belief 22 on choosing entertainment "of the highest quality"; "by beholding we become changed" (2 Corinthians 3:18).
talking.Jehovah's Witness: jw.org counsel on asking whether entertainment features what God hates (Psalm 11:5; Galatians 5:19-21); conscience decides.
talking.Christian Science: "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392); discuss what thoughts a story leaves behind.
talking.Mainline progressive Protestant: Denominational social statements on peace and on war; attention to how the vulnerable are treated; the nuance of lying to protect others.
talking.Orthodox Jewish: The Talmud's allowance of changing the truth for peace in the home (Yevamot 65b) as a discussion point; Torah study valued above entertainment.
talking.Conservative Jewish: Pikuach nefesh (saving life) as a frame for Loid's mission; kind speech and family values applied by each family.
talking.Reform Jewish: Informed autonomy; the prophetic call to justice and peace (Isaiah 2:4).
talking.Muslim: Qur'an on intoxicants (5:90); honesty, with narrow exceptions for reconciliation; the marriage contract (nikah). Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) applies lightly here.
talking.Hindu: Bhagavad Gita on duty; ahimsa (non-harm) and satya (truthfulness) as contrasts to Yor's and Loid's work.
talking.Buddhist: The Five Precepts; karma and whether intent changes the weight of harmful acts; right livelihood.
talking.Shinto: Association of Shinto Shrines, "Principles of Life in Reverence of Kami": sincerity, purity, harmony.
talking.Sikh: Sikh Rehat Maryada; truthful living ("Truth is higher, but higher still is truthful living," Guru Granth Sahib).
talking.Bahá'í: Writings of Bahá'u'lláh and 'Abdu'l-Bahá on truthfulness and world peace; Shoghi Effendi on a "chaste and holy life" (to verify exact wording).
talking.Scientologist: The Way to Happiness precepts ("Take care of children," "Do not murder," "Be worthy of trust").
talking.Wiccan / Pagan: The Wiccan Rede ("An it harm none, do what ye will"); discuss harm done for a "good" cause.
talking.Secular progressive: Common Sense Media's 13+ guide; surveillance states, propaganda and how comedy handles boundaries.
talking.Secular humanist: Humanist Manifesto III on human flourishing and compassion; honesty versus protecting others.
talking.Conservative / traditional: "The good, the true and the beautiful"; duty versus honesty and the story's warning against war.
talking.Satanist: Eleven Satanic Rules of the Earth (on harming children); The Satanic Temple's Seven Fundamental Tenets.
talking.Unitarian Universalist: UUA principles on inherent worth and dignity and on peace and justice.

talking.Catholic: Can a good end justify an evil means (CCC 1753-1756)? What does mercy look like after Tempest is attacked? Compare Rimuru's reviving the dead with Christian hope of resurrection.
talking.Eastern Orthodox: What does taking on the name "Demon Lord" mean for a hero? The passions behind the massacre (grief turned to wrath). Forgiveness as the Church teaches it set beside Rimuru's choices.
talking.Baptist: "Vengeance is mine, says the Lord" set beside Rimuru's choice. Plugged In's film review: "this isn't stuff for the tykes."
talking.Non-denominational Evangelical: Ends and means. Does power make Rimuru good, or does his goodness justify his power? Beneath the Tangles' piece on eating as a starting point.
talking.Pentecostal / Charismatic: Ephesians 6:12 on spiritual powers compared with a story that befriends demons. Why does the story make demons heroes?
talking.Reformed / Presbyterian: The magistrate's sword (Romans 13) versus personal vengeance. Is Rimuru's rule just because he is kind?
talking.Lutheran: What makes defense of a nation lawful? Is entertainment here adiaphora or a matter of conscience for your family?
talking.Methodist / Wesleyan: Would Wesley's "do all the good you can" include the massacre? What does real repentance look like for a ruler?
talking.Anglican / Episcopal: Compare Rimuru with Lewis's rulers in Narnia. When does a "good king" become a tyrant?

that-time-i-got-reincarnated-as-a-slime.weigh: the series strongly endorses tolerance, forgiveness and coexistence across species; but its turning point (ch. 64-68) presents the killing of about 20,000 soldiers to harvest souls as a justified and largely triumphant choice by the hero, with little lasting cost to him. The hero becomes a "Demon Lord," summons a demon from the bodies of the dead, and revives his own dead. The only organized church is shown as hostile and corrupt. Tempest is a benevolent autocracy. On the page: moderate violence, mild fan service, mild language.

the-100-girlfriends.weigh: on the plus side, honesty, fairness, kindness, acceptance of odd and lonely people, and a hero who protects others. On the other side, the story's central claim is that one person rightly dates many partners at once. It is endorsed throughout and never critiqued. Adult school staff are written as partners of a student, a staff member's forced kissing of students is a gag, and a mother and daughter are in the same group. Fan service involves teen and junior-high characters (BBFC; Australian Classification Board; fan wiki chapter titles), and the publisher rates the manga Mature. The content warning makes the Depiction concern Significant for every frame.
sources: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/君のことが大大大大大好きな100人の彼女

On the page: beheadings and body horror (7), child abuse and suicide plans (7), sensual blood scenes and a fireplace undress (5).

the-eminence-in-shadow.weigh: the evil the story names (a cult seeking immortality through a demon, experiments on the sick, corrupt nobles) is clearly framed as evil and defeated. But the hero kills casually and for fun, lies to everyone, and is driven by self-glory; the story treats this mostly as comedy and rewards him, while it also invites readers to laugh at him. The only church is compromised. Fan service is steady but mild in the manga by report, stronger in the anime.

the-fragrant-flower-blooms-with-dignity.weigh: the core message (do not judge by appearance, reconcile divided groups, honesty, kindness, honoring parents) is clear and consistently rewarded; violence is rare and the hero refuses to fight back; there is no sexual content reported, but the series is centered on unchaperoned teen dating, with a private room scene (vol. 19) and a likely kiss (vol. 14) still to confirm; religion is absent except seasonal customs. The main dividing line is teen dating itself, which some traditions counsel against.

the-girl-from-the-other-side.weigh: the message is gentle care for a child, mercy and forgiveness, and a critique of persecution driven by fear; the hero is a dark, horned, devil-like figure ("Dark Is Not Evil"); the human church and its "Heavenly Father" are framed as the source of purges, and both gods are shown as thieves and schemers; souls separate from bodies, and the dead become trees or return to "Mother"; the hero chooses to give up his own life rather than kill another (v8). On the page: little explicit content (no sex, little gore), steady dread and some violence against civilians.

the-quintessential-quintuplets.weigh: the message centers on study, effort, sisterly loyalty, apology and a single faithful choice that ends in marriage (ch. 113, 122), which most traditions read as a good fit; the harem premise turns five girls into rivals for one boy, several kisses happen without consent and are played as romantic (ch. 102-108), Nino's drugging is a gag (ch. 2, 44), and early chapters use fan service of high school girls (vol. 1; CSM: sexual imagery "common"). There is almost no religious content.

the-rising-of-the-shield-hero.weigh: false witness shown as evil and punished; a hero who protects the weak and does not abandon honesty; a hero who buys a child slave and compels her with a magical curse, then raises her as a daughter; anger and vengeance channeled through cursed power; humiliating punishments presented as justice; a religious sect drawn as villainous and heretical, with no positive clergy; a former king given a path to redemption. Every frame should also weigh the Significant depiction items in the Sensitive-content note (a child slave compelled by pain, child torture and a child's death in ch. 21-23, Filo's transformations), which a print check must confirm.

the-seven-deadly-sins.weigh: loyalty, forgiveness and faithful love win; villains are often redeemed; the hero is a demon prince; the highest "god" of the setting and the Demon King are both tyrants; Christian moral names are inverted ("Sins" as heroes, "Commandments" as villains); magic, purgatory, resurrection and reincarnation are real; and the hero's groping of the heroine is played as comedy without consequence. On the page: moderate fantasy violence (6), recurring sexual harassment gags (5), no explicit sex.

three-days-of-happiness.weigh: the story rejects the idea that a life's worth is its price and moves its lead from self-pity to self-giving love; but its premise is selling one's life, and its ending has both leads give up their remaining lives for three days together, which many traditions that hold life as a gift, or that forbid suicide, would see as a real conflict, and which secular reviewers read in opposite ways. On the page: no graphic violence or sex; a sustained suicide-adjacent premise, a planned suicide (Himeno) and a death-by-choice ending.

to-your-eternity.weigh: love and grief are the core; evil (Nokkers, Hayase's obsession, the corrupt church) is framed as harmful; Bon's and Kahaku's self-destruction are framed as love and atonement; reincarnation and spirits of the dead are shown as real; a creator-god figure is distant and ambiguous; the only major church is a persecutor. On the page: frequent death and gore, a predatory obsession with no explicit sex, suicide and self-sacrifice.

toilet-bound-hanako-kun.weigh: on message, wishes are shown as dangerous bargains, a murderer's guilt is taken seriously and atonement through service is offered, and a sacrifice of one girl for another is framed as a horror; but the hero is a ghost of the dead who grants wishes, spirits and exorcism are the world's normal rules, and the heroes cooperate with spirits rather than oppose them. On the page: little sexual content beyond innuendo and one forced kiss, moderate stylized violence, and heavy themes of death, fratricide and a terminal lifespan.

tokyo-revengers.weigh: gang life is shown as giving belonging but ending in death, prison or organized crime; the hero's power is persistence and refusal to abandon anyone, not fighting; revenge is rejected (Baji, ch. 61); nearly everyone is redeemed in the final timeline, including the villain (ch. 278); a Buddhist symbol is used as a gang emblem; suicide appears as both tragedy (Akkun) and loyal sacrifice (Baji). On the page: constant teen violence (8), suicide (7), language, off-page sexual assault, smoking and drinking.

tomie.weigh: lust, envy, vanity and murder are all shown as destructive, and the story never says murder is right; but there is no justice, repentance or redemption, the evil always returns, the sexual exploitation of a 15-year-old by her teacher is part of the first story, an eight-year-old boy is made to kiss her ("Boy"), and critics disagree over whether the stories blame the woman for men's violence (Anime Feminist; Berlatsky) or critique that violence (Taylor via Wikipedia). Because of the content warning, every frame marks the depiction concern Significant. On the page: repeated murder and dismemberment, cannibalism, nude regenerated bodies, a teacher-student sexual relationship (stated in a flashback, not reported as shown), a child kissed ("Boy").

usogui.weigh: the whole story is built on gambling, with lives as stakes; the hero wins by deception, though mostly by exposing others' lies; villains (murderers, corrupt police, a hit-and-run killer, a slaver) are exposed and usually killed under the rules of the wager; there is graphic torture and execution, a child-abuse backstory, loyal friendship, no religion, and a world where an unaccountable private order acts as judge.

witch-hat-atelier.weigh: the heroes are called witches and cast spells, but magic is a drawn craft with no spirits, gods or incantations (Plugged In); misuse of magic is framed as wrong and has grave consequences (ch. 1); forbidden magic on bodies is mostly used by villains; the institution that bans it is shown as partly cruel; one male same-sex couple (vol. 12); a child sexual abuse flashback, condemned (ch. 49); body horror in later volumes. No religion is shown.

yona-of-the-dawn.weigh: trafficking, drug dealing and corrupt rule are framed as evil and opposed; the heroine chooses to serve the people rather than take revenge (Beneath the Tangles; Speculative Faith); the usurper is drawn sympathetically and never simply punished; dragon gods, a god-king and reincarnation are real in the story; violence is protective but frequent and the heroine kills; the romance is chaste. On the page: moderate violence (6), a drug arc, trafficking themes, a suicide in a backstory.
